abstract: Abstract Reeves’ Muntjac ( Muntiacus reevesi ) are an invasive alien species in a number of European and other countries. They listed as a “Species of European Union Concern” requiring member states to survey their populations and undertake management. Muntjac are secretive and existing survey methods are inefficient at low density and cannot reliably provide confidence in species absence. We assess acoustic monitoring as a surveillance method for this species. Muntjac produce readily identifable barking calls in sequences that can last many minutes. We collected 133,227 min of nocturnal recordings using automated sensors from areas known to contain muntjac populations in the UK. These contained 2,453 min containing at least one muntjac call. We developed a machine learning model to automate detection with high precision (F1 = 0.98). Calls were recorded in all months with no clear seasonal pattern. Calls were produced in sequence in sessions with an average duration of over 10 min and could be reliably detected by the sensors over a radius of around 200 m. We recommend 107 h of surveillance per sensor are required to provide 95% confidence that the species is absent from that site. Calling rate can be increased three-fold by the use of playback. We describe how acoustic surveillance can provide complete coverage of an area, a feature that cannot be provided by other methods such as cameras, can be efficient when the species is only present at low density, can provide confidence in absence, and how automation could further improve the cost-effectiveness of this process.
title: Evaluating automated acoustic monitoring for the invasive reeve’s muntjac deer (Muntiacus reevesi): detecting presence, absence and survey design

abstract: Abstract Vocal displays play a key role in mediating intergroup competition among primates, yet the mechanisms through which these signals influence contest outcomes remain unclear. In this study, we investigated close-range vocal encounters among six groups of black howler monkeys ( Alouatta pigra ) in Palenque National Park, Mexico. We used acoustic recordings of 58 intergroup vocal duels. We examined how structural and social features of howling bouts predict success in contests over resources. Our predictors captured three components of vocal interactions: participation (number and identity of callers), synchrony (their temporal alignment), and temporal position (which group initiated or ended the bout and which produced the longest sequence). Bayesian generalized linear mixed models revealed that specific elements of the temporal organization of vocal interactions strongly influenced the likelihood of winning. Groups were more successful when they ended the bout, when adult males terminated simultaneously, when at least one female contributed, when sequences were longer, and when the first call was a roar. Drawn encounters invariably triggered subsequent vocal duels, underscoring the role of repeated signaling in conflict resolution. These findings show that howler monkeys use coordinated and strategically structured vocal behavior as reliable indicators of motivation and cohesion, supporting assessment strategies that reduce costly physical conflicts. Our results highlight the importance of collective motivation, coordination, and persistence of contributions in shaping the dynamics of intergroup competition in primates.
title: Beyond the Final Say: Social Coordination Shapes Success in Howler Monkey (Alouatta pigra) Vocal Duels

abstract: Abstract The vocal repertoire of nonhuman primates contains intergroup vocalizations, which are often transmitted over long distances, and intragroup vocalizations, which are usually transmitted over short distances. Unlike the well-documented intergroup vocalizations of gibbons, which are emitted as loud calls and are specific to species and sex, intragroup vocalizations have received little attention. In this study, we describe the structure of three types of intragroup vocalizations (grunt call, hoo call, and long hoo call) uttered in five contexts (grunt calls during duet, feeding, stress, animals, and attention to humans) in nine northern white-cheeked gibbons ( Nomascus leucogenys ) and five southern yellow-cheeked gibbons ( Nomascus gabriellae ) in zoos. We obtained most data from spontaneous vocalizations across the five contexts, supplemented by recordings during predator model (stress) and preferred food (feeding) presentations. Based on 806 vocalizations, we found that grunt calls were emitted in all contexts, hoo calls were emitted in four contexts and long hoo calls were emitted only in the feeding context. The grunt call structure, which constituted the proportion of the dataset, differed significantly between species and contexts, with significant context-dependent differences in value of the minimum and maximum fundamental frequencies and harmonic structure. Together, these findings highlight the structural and contextual flexibility of intragroup vocalizations in Nomascus gibbons and underscore their potential role in short-range social communication.
title: Intragroup Vocalizations in Captive Northern White-cheeked Gibbons (Nomascus leucogenys) and Southern Yellow-cheeked Gibbons (Nomascus gabriellae)

abstract: Abstract Long-distance vocalizations are crucial for facilitating group coordination and maintaining social relationships in many primates by allowing individuals to exchange information when visual contact is limited. These signals may convey information about both individual identity and social status. We investigated whether lost calls, the primary long-distance contact call of white-faced capuchins ( Cebus imitator ), vary according to caller identity and male dominance rank (alpha vs. subordinate). We quantified multiple acoustic features from 749 lost calls recorded from 24 males and analyzed acoustic variation using permutation-based classification, Random Forest models, and linear mixed-effects analyses. Lost calls showed strong evidence of individual distinctiveness, with classification accuracy significantly above chance and several acoustic features exhibiting greater between-individual than within-individual variation. In contrast, we found little evidence of dominance-related acoustic variation. Multivariate classification of rank did not significantly exceed chance expectations, and univariate analyses revealed no significant differences in fundamental frequency or call duration, with only a modest difference in formant dispersion. These findings indicate that lost calls primarily reflect individual differences rather than dominance-related variation and suggest that receivers infer socially relevant information through individual recognition and prior social knowledge rather than direct acoustic cues to dominance rank. Our results support the importance of vocal individuality in facilitating long-distance communication in socially complex primates.
title: Lost calls vary with individual identity but not dominance rank in male white-faced capuchins (Cebus imitator)

abstract: Pheromone-mediated behaviors are crucial for the survival and reproduction of Drosophila melanogaster, governing activities such as courtship, mating, and aggression. While many studies have focused on short-range interactions involving direct contact between flies, the role of olfactory cues alone in this attraction remains poorly understood. In this study, we investigated the behavioral responses of virgin male and female D. melanogaster to conspecific headspace using a Y-maze. We tested fly responses under various environmental conditions (e.g., in the presence or absence of food odors and with or without social isolation of the tested animals before the experiments). Finally, we repeated some of the experiments in a still-air trap assay. Our results suggest that fly odors may play only a limited role in mate-seeking behavior in D. melanogaster.
title: Drosophila melanogaster Fly Odors Alone are not Sufficient to Attract other Flies

abstract: Abstract Chemical signalling and endocrine state are known to covary with social environment, but the speed of their response to social transitions under natural conditions remains unclear. We examined how major urinary proteins (MUPs) and faecal steroid hormone metabolites respond to shifts between solitary housing and a complex social setting in two house mouse subspecies, Mus musculus musculus and M. m. domesticus . Using repeated sampling in semi-natural enclosures, we measured MUP, testosterone, and corticosterone metabolite concentrations across three contexts: before social exposure, during the social phase, and after return to isolation. Reproductive output was quantified within a 44-day window around each sampling event. Entry into the enclosures triggered a strong, coordinated response: urinary MUP concentrations increased in both sexes and subspecies, paralleled by rises in testosterone and corticosterone metabolites during early social exposure. In males, this pattern reversed rapidly after removal, with MUPs and both hormone metabolites declining within 24 hours of renewed isolation. Under stable social conditions, urinary MUP concentrations increased with current reproductive output, whereas testosterone and corticosterone metabolites showed no such association. MUP concentrations were also unrelated to either hormone, suggesting that socially responsive MUP investment is not directly coupled to steroid levels. Despite baseline differences between subspecies and the expected male bias in MUP production, the main context-dependent patterns were consistent across subspecies. Our results demonstrate pronounced social plasticity in chemical signalling and endocrine state, and indicate that MUP concentrations more closely reflect reproductive outcomes than steroid metabolite concentrations.
title: Social Context Alters Chemical Signalling and Endocrine Profiles in Two Mouse Subspecies

abstract: Aging in insects is characterized by progressive behavioral changes, including declines in locomotion, altered sleep, and disrupted circadian rhythms. The two-spotted cricket ( Gryllus bimaculatus ) is a useful model for behavioral senescence studies because of its experimentally tractable adult lifespan, distinct behavioral repertoire, and ease of laboratory rearing. However, studies simultaneously tracking multiple behaviors across the entire adult lifespan remain limited. In this study, continuous behavioral recordings and DeepLabCut-based markerless pose estimation were used to quantify age-related behavioral changes in eight adult male crickets maintained under a 12:12 h light–dark cycle. Behaviors were classified into locomotion, resting, sleep-like state (SLS), feeding, drinking, and calling, with an additional “others” category. We then assessed age-related changes in hourly and total activity during the light and dark phases by dividing each individual's record into three lifespan-normalized stages—early, mid, and late. Locomotion, resting, and SLS differed significantly between light and dark phases and changed with age. Total distance traveled varied across lifespan segments in a time-of-day dependent manner. Male calling displayed significant light–dark differences and age-related shifts, whereas feeding and drinking showed no detectable differences. Correlation analysis revealed that reductions in calling were associated with increased SLS but not with changes in locomotion, suggesting that declines in reproductive communication may not simply reflect generalized locomotor decline. These findings demonstrate that behavioral aging in adult crickets is behavior-specific rather than a uniform decline, providing a framework for studying behavioral senescence in crickets and other nontraditional insect models.
title: Age-Related Behavioral Changes Across the Adult Lifespan of a Cricket: A Longitudinal Analysis Using DeepLabCut
A metaheuristic-based hybrid approach with grey wolf algorithm and salp swarm algorithm for feature selection in speech emotional classification

abstract: The antifungal activity of halogenated methyl sulfones depends on both the type and number of halogen atoms in the halogenomethylsulfonyl moiety. In this study, 28 halogenomethylphenyl sulfones were evaluated for minimal inhibitory (MIC) and fungicidal concentrations (MFC) against Candida albicans. Active compounds were further tested for cytotoxicity in vitro using the Vero E6 cell line. Notably, 4-(4-chloro-3,4-dichlorophenoxy)-2-nitrophenyl difluoromethyl sulfone (compound 15) showed fungicidal activity while remaining non-toxic at effective doses. Additionally, no adverse effects were observed in Galleria mellonella larvae treated with 15 in vivo. Mechanistic studies with 15 at a sub-inhibitory concentration (2 μg/mL) showed predominant induction of necrosis in C. albicans cells (88.43%) and protoplasts (96.25%), along with increased reactive oxygen species (ROS) production (31.17%). Cell cycle analysis revealed arrest in the G0 phase (99%), consistent with a pro-necrotic mechanism. RT-qPCR indicated that HSP90 gene expression contributes to C. albicans resistance to 15. Confocal microscopy confirmed the compound's fungicidal activity against planktonic and sessile C. albicans cells in vitro. Modulation experiments with exogenous ergosterol showed that reducing sterol concentrations decreased MIC values, suggesting that the fungal cell membrane is the primary target of 15 and that its interaction with ergosterol is critical for activity. Overall, 15 demonstrated antifungal activity comparable to that of amphotericin B and is a promising lead candidate for the development of new antifungal agents for local and systemic candidiasis.
title: Ergosterol-Dependent Membrane Stress and Calcineurin-HSP90 Signaling Govern Fluorinated Sulfone-Induced Cell Death in Candida albicans

abstract: Abstract This essay orbits around an anthropological-cognitive question: who (and what) is the human being to whom human rights should be recognized and with reference to whom these rights are to be tailored in outer space or on other celestial bodies? It is commonly accepted that human rights are universal and therefore must also be applied in outer space or off-Earth environments. The question, however, is whether it is plausible to ontologically postulate the human being independently of its relationship with its environment. The answer provided here is negative. The terrestrial ‘human’ cannot be assumed to be identical to the ‘extraterrestrial human’. This conclusion is articulated from a relational and enactive approach to understanding what the body-mind unity is in the human species. Being—in this case, human being—cannot be considered as distinct from the relational-experiential dimension from which it gushes out in evolutionary terms. And since the evolution of human ‘nature’ is inseparable from the cultural activity of the species Homo sapiens, mediated by the use of language, extraterrestrial humans must be considered a cultural product. If by ‘natural’ we mean something eternal, immutable, ontologically predetermined once and for all, then the ‘human nature’ on which human rights and their application in outer space are based cannot necessarily be ‘unnatural.’ Conversely, from an enactive perspective, off-Earth naturalness is inescapably the consequence of what the mind–body unity does and will do. This draws a line of continuity and circularity between being and ought-to-be, between is and ought, which in outer space comes to the foreground with particular clarity. On the other hand, the exceptional environmental conditions in outer space should be considered as a laboratory for understanding the human condition on Earth. The extreme instability and precariousness of life in outer space demonstrate the adaptive import of human beings’ ability to communicatively universalize (to be intended as the ongoing process of universalis- ing ) their experience through language and the interpenetrative relationship extant between cognition, end-oriented experiential disposition, interactional meaning-making and human rights self-reflexive practice. The answer to the initial question could therefore be: the nature of the human beings to whom human rights must be applied in outer space lies in the future that the above question calls on them to simultaneously mold and discover… including through a determination of the meaning of human rights and their application in outer space. This article aims to investigate this reflexive anthropological circle and its unfolding between Earth and the spaces beyond the sky.
journal: International Journal for the Semiotics of Law - Revue internationale de Sémiotique juridique
title: Rights Without Earth: Dynamics of the Nature/Law Chiasm in Outer Space

abstract: Temple and shrine gardens are ubiquitous features of historical cities in Japan, yet their ponds and small associated waterbodies remain ecologically understudied and may function as urban refugia for anurans. We conducted a systematic assessment of anuran assemblages across culturally managed waterscapes in the Higashiyama area of Kyoto, Japan, surveying 80 waterbodies across 31 facilities. We combined shore-based visual encounter and acoustic surveys with environmental DNA (eDNA) metabarcoding at 43 waterbodies to improve detection under access and disturbance constraints. We recorded seven anuran species and one newt ( Cynops pyrrhogaster ). Glandirana rugosa was the most frequently detected anuran species, followed by Zhangixalus arboreus and Rana tagoi ; these three species were recorded at more waterbodies than the typical paddy-associated species Dryophytes leopardus and Pelophylax nigromaculatus . Breeding was most often confirmed for Z. arboreus , whereas breeding evidence was less frequent for other species. Field surveys and eDNA were complementary: eDNA yielded additional detections of difficult-to-observe species, particularly R. tagoi , while field surveys were essential for confirming reproduction, for example through observations of foam nests. Univariable binomial generalized linear mixed models of species presence/absence, with facility as a random intercept, suggested species-specific associations with local habitat characteristics, including forest proximity and koi ( Cyprinus carpio ) presence. However, several estimates had wide 95% confidence intervals, and the direction and magnitude of the estimated associations differed among species. These results suggest that culturally managed waterbodies can support a distinctive anuran assemblage within the urban landscape and provide a practical baseline for monitoring and managing these potential biocultural refugia in historical cities.
title: Anurans in culturally managed temple and shrine waterscapes in Kyoto: integrated visual, acoustic, and environmental DNA surveys

abstract: Abstract Urban environments impose challenges for wildlife survival, yet some populations show morphological and behavioral adaptations to these novel conditions. The Rufous-collared Sparrow, Zonotrichia capensis, is a neotropical bird that successfully inhabits both urban and wild environments. This study evaluated morphological and song variations of populations in Central Chile and their association with food availability and anthropogenic noise. We measured 34 individuals from the urban and 64 from the wild environment and recorded 46 songs during the breeding season. Food availability and fragmentation were evaluated through primary productivity (NDVI), alongside environmental noise levels. Results show that individuals inhabiting the urban environment have a smaller size, lower body mass, and lower body condition than their conspecifics from wild environments. Furthermore, song structure shows an increase in the minimum frequencies in the urban population, where we registered higher noise levels. These findings suggest that continuous food availability, higher fragmentation, and anthropogenic noise in the city explain the morphological and vocal divergence observed in urban populations compared to wild ones.
title: City birds are smaller but noisier: morphology, body condition, and song variation between Rufous-collared Sparrows (Zonotrichia capensis) from urban and wild environments in Central Chile

abstract: Aquatic habitats are increasingly endangered by oxyfluorfen (OXY), a diphenyl ether herbicide that induces hepatotoxicity and oxidative stress in aquatic organisms. Banana (Musa acuminata) peel, a valuable byproduct, is known for its antioxidant properties; however, its potential to counteract OXY-induced liver toxicity in Oreochromis niloticus remains unexplored. Therefore, this study investigated the hepatoprotective effects of banana peel powder (BPP) against OXY-induced liver damage and the underlying pathways. A hepatotoxicity model was implemented by subjecting O. niloticus to OXY (0.33 mg/L) for 9 weeks, with or without dietary BPP supplementation (20 g/kg). To assess hepatic injury, oxidative stress, lipid metabolism, and biochemical alterations, hepatic histopathological examination, and real-time quantitative PCR analyses were conducted. Outcomes revealed that OXY exposure disrupted lipid and protein profiles, as evidenced by increased blood cholesterol and triglycerides and reduced serum protein levels. In addition, an elevation in bilirubin content, liver functional enzymes, and lipid peroxides (malondialdehyde), with a lowering of antioxidant enzymes, was observed in the OXY-exposed fish. Moreover, OXY induced upregulation of endoplasmic reticulum stress and apoptotic-related genes (ire-1α, xbp-1, atf-6, eif-2α, chop, and jnk). In addition to that, histopathological investigation of hepatic tissues demonstrated severe hepatic degeneration, peripancreatic hemorrhage, necrosis, and congestion. Notably, dietary BPP improves antioxidant response, lipid metabolism, and liver structure, while alleviating hepatocyte damage and disrupted gene expression. Overall, BPP (20 g/kg) may protect O. niloticus against OXY-induced liver damage through its antioxidant potential, supporting its application as a functional additive in aquaculture.
title: Dietary banana peels modulate waterborne oxyfluorfen-induced hepatotoxicity in Nile tilapia (Oreochromis niloticus) via regulation of redox homeostasis and ER stress signaling

abstract: Rising nickel (Ni) and copper (Cu) pollution in water bodies has the potential to alter fish physiology and undermine aquaculture sustainability. A valuable byproduct, the watermelon rind (Citrullus lanatus), has potent antioxidant properties. However, its hepatoprotective role against Ni + Cu co-exposure in Nile tilapia (Oreochromis niloticus) remains uninvestigated. Hence, this study assessed the efficacy of dietary C. lanatus rind powder (CLRP) in safeguarding against liver damage induced by Ni + Cu. Fish (37.30 ± 0.20 g) were assigned to four groups: control, CLRP (40 g/kg diet), Ni + Cu (3.60 and 3.35 mg/L), and CLRP + Ni+Cu for 45 days. Findings showed hepatic dysfunction, as evidenced by increased liver enzymes and reduced protein fractions concurrent with Ni and Cu exposure. In addition, disruption of the lipid profile (increased triglycerides and cholesterol) and elevation of bilirubin fractions were evident in the Ni + Cu group. Simultaneous exposure to Ni and Cu induced suppression of antioxidant enzyme activities (superoxide dismutase, catalase, and glutathione peroxidase), besides the elevation of malondialdehyde levels. Microscopic analysis of hepatic tissue showed hepatocyte necrosis and degeneration as well as dilation of the portal veins. Furthermore, the co-occurring exposure altered the antioxidant signaling pathway (nrf2/keap1). It also downregulated immune function genes (il10 and ctsb) and upregulated stress response genes (hsp70 and hsp90). Importantly, CLRP supplementation notably strengthens antioxidant capacity, supports lipid metabolism, and maintains liver architecture. Additionally, it reduces hepatocyte injury and transcriptional disruptions. Overall, CLRP (40 g/kg) shows promise in protecting Nile tilapia against Ni + Cu combined exposure, supporting its use as a feed additive in aquaculture.
authors: Abdullah K. Alguaimi Abdullah K. Alguaimi
title: Dietary watermelon (Citrullus lanatus) rind mitigates nickel- and copper-induced hepatic, metabolic, and nrf2/keap1 signaling disruptions in Nile tilapia (Oreochromis niloticus)
Adsorption Process of Two Fruit Fly Drosophila melanogaster Pheromones On Human Olfactory Receptor Using Statistical Physics, DFT Quantum Calculation and Molecular Docking Analysis

abstract: Abstract Echolocation is a biological adaptation that can be influenced by body mass (Mb). To cope with seasonal changes in ambient temperature (Ta) and food availability, bats either increase Mb to hibernate or reduce it to remain active during winter and minimize energy expenditure. In bats that remain active throughout the year, seasonal changes in Mb may affect echolocation traits. We analyzed Mb and echolocation pulses of Eptesicus fuscus captured in La Malinche National Park, a montane ecosystem in central Mexico, during the dry-cold and dry-warm seasons. We examined the relationship between Mb, season and Ta, and four echolocation variables: maximum frequency, peak frequency, minimum frequency, and bandwidth. Our results revealed a positive relationship between Mb and season and Ta, and a negative relationship between Mb and all four echolocation variables. These findings suggest that seasonal variation in echolocation traits, associated to changes in Mb, has important ecological implications enabling bats to adjust to changing prey availability. During the dry-warm season, larger bats with lower frequencies and narrower bandwidths may reduce acoustic resolution without substantially compromising foraging efficiency in prey-rich environments. In contrast smaller bats with higher-resolution calls may enhance prey detection when sources are limited during the dry-cold season. Future avenues of research on this topic are discussed.
title: Seasonal shifts in body mass shape echolocation traits in Eptesicus fuscus from central Mexico

abstract: Abstract The common brushtail possum is a major invasive species in New Zealand, damaging native ecosystems and agricultural systems and is a target of the national Predator Free 2050 eradication programme. Reliable, low-cost monitoring is critical to this programme, and acoustic detection offers a scalable alternative to traditional trapping and camera-based methods. The bioacoustics approach to automated brushtail possum detection using deep learning models suffers from excessive false alarms. At the same time, the high computational demands of the most accurate models make them unsuitable for resource-limited edge devices. In this paper, a targeted hard-negative mining method, Cross-Model Confusion Mapping (CMCM), is proposed to overcome these problems. It uses the error profile of a pre-trained model to identify bird calls most frequently misclassified as possum vocalisations. These bird calls are then relabelled and added to the training data. Three CMCM audiosets were generated and compared with size-matched sets assembled through untargeted sampling. CNNs with 3, 5, 7, 10, and 13 layers were trained using identical augmentation pipelines. Experiments showed that CMCM-trained models maintain accuracy while significantly reducing false alarms. In particular, the 10-layer CMCM-trained CNN achieved the most reliable detection with zero false positives. The inference times are orders of magnitude faster, with substantially lower computational demand, than the state-of-the-art Audio Spectrogram Transformer. These findings suggest that CMCM enables accurate, low-latency possum detection suitable for real-time deployment on edge devices. The method is generalisable to other bioacoustic detection tasks where false positives arise from acoustically similar non-target species.
title: Cross-Model Confusion Mapping: False Alarm Minimisation in Possum Call Detection Using Deep Learning

abstract: Abstract Humpback whales ( Megaptera novaeangliae ) undertake long-distance annual migrations to access seasonally optimal habitats for feeding and reproduction. However, shifts in migration timing have been documented across multiple populations worldwide. Under rapid environmental change and increasing coastal development, there is growing concern that long-distance migrants may arrive in critical habitats outside favourable ecological windows. Along Australia’s east coast, the E1 subpopulation migrates between Antarctic feeding grounds and Coral Sea breeding areas, yet substantial geographic gaps remain in monitoring their occurrence, particularly along their migration route. To address this, a passive acoustic recorder was deployed throughout the migratory period in Batemans Bay, NSW from May to September 2024. Across 102,960 min of acoustic monitoring, humpback whale vocalisations were detected in 70% of monitored hours, spanning 87% of monitored days. The first detection occurred on 19 May, with sustained daily presence from 22 May through late September. Acoustic presence increased rapidly from late May and peaked in early August, before increasing again towards the end of the monitoring period in late September. Detections were significantly higher at dawn (73%), dusk (73%), and night (80%) compared to day (62%). These findings provide the first systematic account of humpback whale occurrence in Batemans Bay and update current understanding of humpback whale migration timing along the NSW south coast, including the timing of the northward migration after more than a decade. The consistently high acoustic presence observed throughout the monitoring period indicates that Batemans Bay represents an important migratory habitat for E1 humpback whales travelling along Australia’s east coast.
title: Passive Acoustic Monitoring Reveals Sustained Presence of Humpback Whales (Megaptera novaeangliae) in Batemans Bay, New South Wales, Australia, During Migration Season
Decoding the roar: insights into acoustic detection and attenuation of Asiatic lions’ vocal behaviour

abstract: Music Emotion Recognition (MER) is vital for understanding emotional responses to music and advancing aesthetic education, enhancing artistic sensitivity and cognitive growth. However, current MER methods frequently fail to effectively model cross-modal emotional dependencies and the dynamic variations in expressive cues. This research proposes a multimodal deep learning (DL) framework that integrates the Multimodal Music Emotion dataset including 14 audios file (70 records), textual data (2000 records), and visual elements (2000 records) modalities for accurate MER and comprehensive evaluation of aesthetic education effectiveness. Preprocessing audio signals includes noise reduction, and features are extracted using Mel-Frequency Cepstral Coefficients (MFCCs) to be acoustic and timbral structures. Textual lyrics are preprocessed through tokenization, and word embeddings capture semantic and emotional context in features. Visual data is resized, and features Visual sentiment is interpreted using a convolutional neural network (CNN) that extracts face expression cues. A feature-level fusion approach combined with an attention mechanism highlights emotionally dominant attributes across modalities. The proposed Adaptive Golden Jackal-driven Dynamic Graph Neural Network (AdapGJ-DGNNet) dynamically constructs graph relationships among multimodal feature nodes and adaptively updates edge weights using the AdapGJ strategy, enabling optimal graph connectivity and robust temporal-spatial emotion modeling. The DGNNet structure facilitates learning non-linear correlations between modalities and enhances generalization under complex emotional variations. The proposed AdapGJ-DGNNet achieves 90.12% accuracy, 85.47% recall, 87.05% F1-score, and a ROC–AUC of 0.989, outperforming all baseline methods, with results validated through an efficient Python-based implementation. This research highlights the potential of intelligent multimodal MER systems for advancing aesthetic education.
title: A model for music emotion recognition and aesthetic education effect evaluation based on deep learning and multimodal data

abstract: Drama teaching helps in the development of creativity, communication, teamwork, and expressiveness but evaluation usually based on subjective observation. Creativity, expressiveness, teamwork, and performance outcomes cannot be objectively measured due to the absence of the Adaptive assessment. To solve this, the study suggests Deep Learning (DL) and Internet of Things (IoT)-optimized framework to assess teaching in theatres and offer adaptive feedback. The IoT-based sensors, such as wearable sensors, motion sensors, and microphones, record multimodal data when participating in drama games, including verbal expressions, bodily movements, gestures, and physiological reactions. Z-score normalization is used as data preprocessing and Independent Component Analysis (ICA) is used as spatial feature extractor of posture and gesture data. Students, such as tone, gestures and interactions, to extract the complex patterns of expressivity and dependence between multimodal features, use another model, Self-Attention-Refined Generative Adversarial Network (SATT-GAN) model, to pay attention to the key elements of dramatic input. This guarantees accurate, context-specific feedback. The GAN component produces realistic, adaptive performance recommendations, including changing the tone, stage movement, or group coordination, and offers a smart, immersive, and tailored learning experience. Scalable Golden Jackal Optimization (SGJO) picks the most relevant attributes and optimizes hyper parameters to achieve the best evaluation. The model is applied to smart classrooms with Python, providing educators and learners with dynamic feedback on expressiveness, teamwork, creativity, interest, and learning outcomes. The experimental results demonstrate that the proposed SATT-GAN-SGJO framework achieves high predictive performance with an accuracy of 97.5%, precision of 95.2%, recall of 95.7%, F1-score of 96.3%, and specificity of 96.8%, confirming its effectiveness in objectively evaluating drama instruction outcomes. Seamless integration of IoT data collection and adaptive feedback through the DL can assist teachers in their teaching, and give students a more enjoyable drama learning experience.
title: A deep learning and IoT assisted framework for evaluating drama instruction outcomes

abstract: High-Performance Computing (HPC) systems have become integral to scientific discovery and Artificial Intelligence (AI), yet their complex, distributed architectures expose them to sophisticated cyber threats capable of disrupting large-scale computational workflows. Traditional intrusion detection systems (IDS) lack the adaptability and contextual understanding required to secure such dynamic environments. This study presents an advanced cybersecurity framework that leverages a Graph-Temporal Transformer Network (GTTN) combined with a Hybrid Adaptive Meta-Optimization (HAMO) algorithm to enhance anomaly detection and classification in HPC infrastructures. The proposed framework first constructs graph representations of inter-node communications and process-level dependencies, capturing both structural and temporal relationships within HPC traffic. A self-supervised pretraining phase is employed to learn normal behavioral patterns without labeled data, improving the model’s resilience to zero-day attacks. The fine-tuned GTTN then integrates spatial attention and temporal encoding to detect deviations indicative of intrusion activities. To further optimize model performance, the HAMO algorithm, which fuses the exploration capability of the Spotted Hyena Optimizer (SHO) with the exploitation strength of the Whale Optimization Algorithm (WOA), is applied to adaptively tune the network’s hyperparameters. Experimental evaluations conducted on HPC-tailored versions of the CIC-IDS 2018 and LANL Cyber dataset reveal that the proposed system achieves detection accuracies of 0.995 and 0.982, outperforming state-of-the-art deep learning (DL) and evolutionary baselines. The framework also demonstrates reduced false alarm rates and superior scalability under high-throughput workloads. These results indicate that the integration of graph-temporal learning and hybrid meta-optimization provides a powerful and adaptive defense strategy for next-generation HPC cybersecurity, offering practical potential for deployment in exascale computing environments.
journal: International Journal of Computational Intelligence Systems
title: Enhancing Cybersecurity in Smart High-Performance Computing Systems Using Graph-Temporal Deep Learning and Hybrid Optimization

abstract: Detecting fraud in distributed financial transaction systems is challenging. It is extremely rare to find a fraudulent record. The interactions among transactional records have a relational structure and the data can’t be stored centrally by every participating institution. The paper introduces the federated graph learning framework i.e. GenOpt-FedGNN. The framework combines Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) with client local learning, graph neural classification, and the aggregation of the trained models through adaptive process of Grey Wolf Optimization (GWO) and Asteroid Satellite Inspired Optimization (ASIO). Each client preprocesses their own transactions independently, produces more minority fraud samples to train a class weighted Graph Neural Network (GNN), and builds a transaction graph. Each client sends updates regarding model and validator to the server. The framework is tested with a set of 200,000 PaySim transactions. Transactions were randomly sampled and distributed among the five distributed clients with 30 communication rounds. Six configurations (FedAvg, GWO and ASIO with and without GAN augmentation), have been compared by Accuracy, Balanced Accuracy, Precision, Recall, F1-score, ROC-AUC, PR-AUC, Specificity, False Positive Rate, False Negative Rate and Confusion-matrix measures. The ablation analysis demonstrated that GAN augmentation doubled local fraud training samples and reduced class-imbalance ratio. But, the local fraud data has been extremely imbalanced. Overall, at the final round, the accuracy was highest with ASIO-GAN (96.40%), the specificity (96.41%), precision (1.58%), F1-score (3.11%), and the lowest False Positive Rate (3.59%). The best Balanced Accuracy (94.16%) was found for FedAvg-GAN, and the best PR-AUC (60.02%) was found for ASIO-NoGAN. The GWO GAN-based configurations got best PR-AUC of 59.20%. The ablation results on the other hand further showed that using GAN for augmentation resulted in a consistent increase in the Accuracy, Precision, F1-Score, Specificity and false alarm control compared to using it without GAN. So augmentation with GAN and aggregation with Adaptive Aggregation can affect the sensitivity–specificity trade-off but not necessarily all the other aggregation metrics. The proposed framework is reproducible and data local to the raw data for the graph-based fraud detection application which features extreme class imbalance.
journal: International Journal of Computational Intelligence Systems
title: GenOpt-FedGNN: GAN-Augmented Federated Graph Learning with GWO and ASIO-Inspired Adaptive Aggregation for Imbalanced Fraud Detection

abstract: India’s Project Cheetah (2022–2025) is a significant, high-stakes translocation effort aimed at re-establishing the cheetah (Acinonyx jubatus) seven decades after its local extinction. This study employs concepts of sociotechnical imaginary and epistemic injustice to analyze the project's contested outcomes, with a focus on the interaction between scientific risk and governance failure. Project Cheetah reached a key milestone with the birth of 22 cubs; however, it was also marked by high initial mortality. By April 2025, the project recorded the loss of 8 adult founder cheetahs (40.0% of the original 20) and 5 cubs (22.7%). Although conservation efforts inherently involve biological risks, our analysis shows that the observed mortality rate exceeded expected ecological thresholds, with a significant concentration around institutional instability. An analysis of cheetah mortality patterns revealed a negative association between survival time and the period immediately following a critical change in project coordination, suggesting that governance disruptions may have contributed to increased mortality. This was worsened by a strong national sociotechnical imaginary of ecological revival, which often overshadowed transparent risk communication and scientific criticism. Limited stakeholder consultation and asymmetric information created conditions for testimonial and hermeneutical injustices, marginalizing the expertise of critical voices. The study concludes that the long-term success of large-scale, transnational rewilding projects depends heavily on institutional capacity, not just ecological suitability. Lessons learned highlight the importance of transparent data management, thorough and inclusive consultation, and honest communication of scientific uncertainty to stakeholders, building the trust needed to sustain such complex political and environmental initiatives.
title: Understanding social and scientific conflicts shaping modern wildlife conservation

abstract: Group departures in social animals require coordination in time and space. Movement cues are important, but many species vocalize in relation to departure, indicating that the relevant information can be multimodal. Here, the use of vocalizations in relation to visual cues was investigated in three groups of western gorillas, Gorilla gorilla , in the Central African Republic. Grunt and grumbles were the common call types. Grumbles were mostly produced by initiators typically just after a departure was initiated. By contrast, grunts were equally produced by initiators and followers, but here the peak was observed just before departure. Grunts were produced by individuals adopting different body postures. Individuals producing grunts while lying on the ground were slower to move than those sitting or standing, indicating that call–posture combinations provided information about an individual's likelihood to move. Finally, initiations were more likely to succeed when more individuals vocalized, which is consistent with shared decision-making. The results of this study indicate that gorilla departure decisions rest on multimodal information, showing the mechanism by which social animals may solve collective action problems without language.
title: Multimodal coordination of group departures in western gorillas

abstract: The temporal structure of an animal's vocal output can be cognitively controlled: a feature of particular interest in vocal learning species, which actively modify and diversify their vocalizations. Although birdsong is the most thoroughly studied aspect of animal communication, its rhythms remain largely unknown. Here, we revisit the question of vocal individuality in the songs of male yellowhammers, Emberiza citrinella , purely from a rhythmic perspective. Yellowhammers use simple songs composed of two phrases: the initial phrase, with one individual usually having a repertoire of on average two such phrase types, and the dialect phrase, which contains the dialect that is the same for all males at a given locality. Some of the initial phrases are commonly shared between various males, but their combinations and frequency contours are individually unique and temporally stable. Using focal recordings of 38 known individuals collected over 3 years in the same geographical location, we calculated a set of nine temporal indices to describe each song and compared individuals in a permuted discriminant function analysis. Subsequently, we calculated the potential for individual coding for each of these parameters. To assess whether rhythmic similarity may depend on the singers' proximity, we calculated vocal dissimilarity as the Euclidean distances between each pair of males and used Kendall's correlation to test the relationship between acoustic and geographical distance between them. We show that yellowhammer males use individual rhythms, maintained across different phrase types and carried mostly in the variability of the inter-onset interval and syllable rate, measured as syllables/s, within the song. There were particularly strong rhythmic differences between singers among the closest neighbours, which decreased over the first 600 m. There was no pattern for neighbours beyond this distance. This study is the first to demonstrate the existence of strong individuality based purely on rhythm, as well as rhythmic differentiation from neighbours, in a songbird.
title: Yellowhammer males sing using individual isochronous rhythms and maximize rhythmic dissimilarity with neighbours

abstract: Human communication relies on a distinct capacity for social interaction, underpinned by cognitive skills like intentionality. To communicate intentionally, signallers produce signals with the explicit goal of influencing the behaviour or the mental states of receivers. Although long thought to be uniquely human, comparative studies have provided evidence consistent with first-order intentional communication (i.e. the signaller intends to change the recipient’s behaviour) in great apes and some monkey species. Despite being cooperative breeders like humans and renowned for their sophisticated vocal and cognitive skills, common marmosets, Callithrix jacchus , are still largely unstudied with respect to the intentional nature of their gestural communication. Here, we thus aimed to increase our understanding of common marmosets’ intentional abilities by studying communicative interactions of 20 adult individuals living in four different groups in a semiarid environment in Brazil. We especially focused on the context of grooming, a crucial context for the exchange of signals, and investigated the presence and role of gestures and whether these were aligned with intentional communication patterns. From focal animal sampling and video footage, we found that marmosets produced three different gestures (Touch, Roll-over and Present) both to initiate grooming and during ongoing interactions. These findings suggest that intentional communication plays a crucial role in the cooperative interactions of common marmosets, showing that flexible, goal-directed signalling is not restricted to the vocal domain or great apes, but may be a convergent trait driven by the demands of a cooperative social lifestyle.
title: The role of intentional communication in monkeys: evidence from gestural signalling in common marmosets in the wild

abstract: Group living requires individuals to make their internal states perceptible to sustain coordination and cohesion. Multimodal signals may efficiently convey such socioemotional information. Although often considered reflexive, yawning exhibits structural variability and can trigger contagion, suggesting communicative potential. In humans and geladas, Theropithecus gelada , yawns can include a vocal component that alone triggers yawn contagion, yet the reasons behind its emergence remain underexplored. We conducted the first systematic study of vocalized yawns in geladas, analysing over 2500 yawns from nearly 200 wild and captive individuals to test whether multimodal yawning reflects affective states. Using Bayesian modelling, we tested hypotheses linking yawn vocalizations to emotional valence, arousal or motor by-products. Multimodal yawns were more frequent in adult males, who face greater socioemotional demands, and were strongly associated with high-arousal contexts: they occurred most often after aggression, copulations and greetings, less during grooming and least during rest. Moreover, yawn vocalizations often co-occurred with other species-specific affiliative calls, which are known to index arousal and maintain cross-sex bonds, indicating integration within the species' broader communicative system. Our findings indicate that yawn vocalizations may act as socioemotional signals, amplifying arousal and integrating into the species’ vocal repertoire. By externalizing internal states, they could enhance emotional attunement, synchrony and social cohesion in complex social groups.
title: Multimodal yawns signal emotional arousal in geladas

abstract: Distinguishing between own and alien young is an important part of mammalian maternal behaviour. The mechanisms and the sensory cues involved depend on the species' natural ecology and have been particularly well studied in herd- and colony-living species. However, research in solitary-living carnivores, where mothers typically hide their altricial young, is largely lacking. We studied vocal individuality of separation cries of kittens of the domestic cat, Felis silvestris catus , and examined whether mothers distinguished between the vocalizations of their own and alien kittens under seminatural conditions. We tested 13 domestic cat mothers when their kittens were 3 and 6 weeks old to determine whether vocal or spatial cues influenced the mothers' approach by playing back separation cries, either from their own or alien kittens, broadcast either from the nest or from a different location. We found no evidence that mothers discriminated between the cries of their own and alien kittens, despite considerable vocal individuality among them. When the kittens were 3 weeks old, mothers were immediately alerted by playbacks of separation cries, whether from their own or alien kittens, and whether played from the nest or another location, but mainly approached the playbacks when they originated from their nest. When the kittens were 6 weeks old, mothers increasingly approached playbacks from different locations, although still without differentiating between cries based on the callers’ identities. We conclude that this pattern of maternal response aligns well with the ecology of this naturally solitary, obligate carnivore and the developmental stages of its young.
title: Location over voice: cues used by cat mothers to return to their kittens

abstract: Communication networks are widespread across species, permitting information flow and facilitating social connections across space and time. In birds, communication networks are well studied in territorial species, with long-range songs connecting individuals across space, and where unintended listeners extract information from others’ signalling interactions. Yet, acoustic signals also play important social roles at short range, forming communication networks that connect individuals within larger social units. Wild zebra finches provide a unique model system to examine such communication networks in a nonterritorial species. Zebra finches breed in loose colonies in the Australian arid zone, move around in pairs or small groups and gather at social hotspots, thus forming dynamic, potentially multilevel, societies. Here, we quantified singing activity and connectivity using the individually distinctive male song recorded at two breeding colonies and three social hotspots over 1–3 days. We identified 1835 song bouts from 163 males based on spectrographic similarities and assessed within- and between-individual song assignments with a deep-learning model (BirdNET). We constructed communication networks based on temporal singing proximity at shared locations: social hotspots and breeding colonies. We reveal higher singing activity at social hotspots than at breeding sites, with almost no dawn song at either site. Singing peaked later, yet at different times of day, between breeding sites and social hotspots. Communication networks, with distinct males singing in close temporal proximity, were apparent in both contexts, with larger networks at hotspots. These networks included some individuals that sang together repeatedly at either site, but overall networks were not strongly nested, with only very few males maintaining associations across breeding colonies and hotspots. These networks may facilitate synchronized foraging and breeding as adaptations to a harsh and unpredictable environment. Additionally, our approach offers a novel road map for widening the understanding of communication networks.
title: Communication networks of wild zebra finches, Taeniopygia castanotis

abstract: Animal populations often exhibit complex patterns of spatial or social structure, with various levels of organization below the population level. Acoustic monitoring can reveal such structure, particularly when animals produce calls that contain individual or group-level signatures. In this study, we monitored the complex contact calls of belugas, Delphinapterus leucas , in the St Lawrence Estuary, Canada, across six sites during five field seasons. Using a mark–recapture-based movement network, we examined the movement of belugas by tracking the occurrence of distinctive contact calls across sites. Our movement network revealed a high degree of population structure and the presence of two distinct communities: one within the Saguenay Fjord, recorded at two locations (i.e. the ‘Saguenay community’), and another along the southern shore of the estuary, recorded at four locations (i.e. the ‘South Shore community’). These results align with findings of a previous photo-identification-based study that suggested the presence of clusters of individuals inhabiting the Saguenay Fjord and southern shore of the estuary. Our study provides the first acoustic evidence of fine-scale population structure in the endangered St Lawrence Estuary beluga population. These findings, together with the population's exposure to significant anthropogenic disturbances across its range, reinforce the need to expand the Saguenay–St Lawrence Marine Park to protect the core habitats and home ranges of both communities. More broadly, our results demonstrate that passive acoustic monitoring can reveal population spatial structure and inform behaviour-driven conservation action.
title: From calls to communities: acoustic monitoring of contact calls indicates spatial structure in endangered belugas

abstract: In animal communication, including human conversation, vocal exchange is a key phenomenon that organizes interactions so that partners exchange rapidly, taking turns and avoiding overlapping vocalizations. By contrast, vocal exchanges in cetaceans have generally been reported to involve frequent overlapping vocalizations. However, it remains unclear whether animals overlap their vocalizations incidentally or actively. Here, we explored the behavioural mechanisms underlying vocal overlapping during vocal exchange in common bottlenose dolphins, Tursiops truncatus . We first identified the signature whistles of five captive dolphins and then conducted a playback experiment in which a separated individual's signature whistle was played to dolphins housed together in the focal pool. The observed rate of vocal overlap was significantly higher than expected by chance, indicating that overlap did not occur incidentally. Analysis of spontaneously produced signature whistle sequences showed that dolphins produced whistles with isochronous timing, and that this isochrony exceeded that of a random model. This indicates that dolphins naturally produce signature whistles isochronously. We then evaluated two possible explanations for vocal overlap: dolphins might overlap by predicting the timing of a partner's next whistle, or by responding rapidly after hearing the next whistle, even before it had ended. However, in a playback experiment comparing vocal responses to isochronous versus nonisochronous sequences, the frequency of overlapping did not differ between conditions. This suggests that isochronous temporal regularities in vocal sequences did not facilitate prediction of the timing of the partner's next whistle and that vocal overlap is better explained by rapid responses following detection of conspecific whistles. These findings suggest that bottlenose dolphins, like other taxa, exchange vocalizations to reduce response delay. However, unlike most other species, they do not avoid overlapping and instead incorporate it into the vocal exchange. This study provides new comparative insight into both the universality and the diversity of vocal exchange patterns across species.
title: Testing mechanisms underlying vocal overlap during vocal exchange of signature whistles in common bottlenose dolphins
How does domestication shape responses to communicative cues? Evidence from a novel marker task in dogs and dingoes

abstract: When we hear a person's voice, we can often infer attributes such as age or identity, even without seeing the speaker. This ability suggests the presence of a cross-modal representation that integrates information from both the visual and auditory modalities. Such representations are not limited to interactions within the same species but also occur between different species. Previous studies have shown that dogs, Canis familiaris , can match human voices with faces based on familiarity, sex and emotional expression. However, it remains unclear whether they can distinguish humans by age across modalities. Such ability could be important for dogs to adapt their behaviour appropriately towards children versus adults in everyday interactions. This study investigated whether dogs can form cross-modal representations of human adults and children using an expectancy-violation paradigm. We hypothesized that if dogs possess such representations, they would exhibit longer looking times during voice–face mismatched (incongruent) trials compared to voice–face matched (congruent) trials for both adult and child stimuli. The experiment involved seating dogs in front of a monitor. Immediately after hearing the voice of an adult woman or a girl played through a speaker, the dogs were shown a photograph of a face that either matched or mismatched the voice. We then measured gaze duration towards the monitor. Contrary to our prediction, dogs tended to look longer in congruent than in incongruent conditions, although this effect was only marginally significant. This pattern suggests that dogs may discriminate between congruent and incongruent voice–face pairings, but not in the predicted direction. Exploratory analyses further suggested that this tendency was more pronounced among dogs who had lived with children. Overall, these findings provide tentative evidence that dogs may associate human female voices and faces across age classes, and that experience with children could influence this process.
title: Dogs might associate the voices and faces of human girls and adult women
Reinforcement drives the evolution of increased variation in temperature-driven acoustic plasticity

abstract: Purpose To investigate the effects of narrowband blue and green light on refractive development in guinea pigs and to explore the associations of retinal and serum dopamine (DA) and melatonin. Design Experimental animal study. Participants Seventy-two 2-week-old pigmented male guinea pigs. Methods Animals were randomly assigned to white (5000 K), blue (430 nm), or green (530 nm) light for 12 weeks. A longitudinal cohort (n=15 per group) underwent biweekly measurements of refractive error, axial length (AL), and choroidal thickness (ChT). Separate terminal cohorts were euthanized at weeks 0, 4, and 12 (n=3 per group per time point) for measurement of serum and retinal dopamine (DA), melatonin, and scleral type I collagen. In vitro, primary scleral fibroblasts were treated with DA, melatonin, and pathway inhibitors to assess cAMP, cGMP, and type I collagen levels. Main Outcome Measures Refractive error, axial length, choroidal thickness, retinal and serum dopamine and melatonin levels, scleral type I collagen content, and in vitro type I collagen levels. Results In the longitudinal cohort, at 12 weeks, blue light exposure shifted refractive development toward greater hyperopia (+1.67 ± 0.14 D) and reduced AL elongation (−0.08 ± 0.07 mm) compared with white and green light (both P < 0.001), while green light exposure shifted refractive development toward greater myopia (−2.42 ± 0.14 D) and AL elongation (+0.69 ± 0.11 mm). ChT increased under blue light (+14.80 ± 10.35 μm) and decreased under green light (−19.25 ± 4.39 μm; P < 0.001). In the separate terminal cohorts, blue light was associated with significantly higher serum and retinal DA levels at 4 and 12 weeks compared with white and green light ( P < 0.05). Melatonin levels showed no sustained intergroup differences. In vitro, DA increased type I collagen levels, an effect enhanced by adenylyl cyclase inhibition, whereas melatonin reduced type I collagen levels. Conclusions Narrowband blue and green light are associated with opposing refractive and axial growth patterns in guinea pigs, accompanied by differences in dopamine levels and scleral collagen content. These findings support a dopamine-related contribution to wavelength-dependent refractive development and suggest that spectral composition may influence ocular growth. Further studies are needed to establish causality and evaluate translational potential for myopia prevention.
journal: Advances in Ophthalmology Practice and Research
title: Narrowband Blue and Green Light Are Associated with Opposing Refractive Effects and Dopamine Signaling in Guinea Pigs

abstract: Passive Acoustic Monitoring has become a cornerstone of marine mammal conservation, enabling continuous, non-invasive monitoring through the detection and analysis of vocalizations. As the focus shifts from retrospective analyses to real-time monitoring, classification systems must operate within the strict computational constraints of ultra-low-power embedded devices, generalize across diverse acoustic environments, remain robust to anthropogenic noise from vessel traffic, and classify distinct beluga sound types to enable advanced ecological analyses such as abundance estimation and behavioral inference. We address these challenges by developing a classification model for the endangered beluga whale population of the St. Lawrence Estuary. Our lightweight, quantized convolutional neural network classifies beluga vocalizations under natural field conditions, including overlapping calls and variable background noise. The model achieves a macro-averaged F1 score of 0.85 with a memory footprint of under 512 kilobytes, satisfying the constraints of edge-deployable microcontrollers. Using labeled examples with and without vessel noise, we directly quantified the impact of anthropogenic interference, revealing a drop to an F1 score of 0.75 in the presence of boat noise. Training on data from four distinct sites, we demonstrate that a single multi-site model generalizes effectively across all locations. In a leave-one-site-out evaluation, the full-precision model maintains strong performance on unseen sites with an average F1 drop of only 0.05, while the quantized model shows a larger gap of 0.10, highlighting the increased sensitivity of compressed models to distribution shifts.
title: Lightweight beluga call classification under habitat variability and marine traffic noise

abstract: Sperm whales ( Physeter macrocephalus ) produce powerful broadband echolocation clicks for navigation and foraging, which are detectable over several kilometers in the ocean. Accurate range and depth localization of the whale source using these clicks is important for behavioral studies, to determine population size, and explore effects of, e.g., anthropogenic activities. As a practical, easy to deploy setup, we consider for localization a two hydrophone array vertically deployed from, e.g., a small vessel or buoy. Unlike existing approaches that perform localization per click, our solution exploits the sequential structure of sperm-whale echolocation clicks to formalize the localization solution as a hidden Markov model (HMM) whose states encode the whale’s range and depth. Emission probabilities are derived by the similarity between the expected and measured time-difference-of-arrival between the direct and first reflection paths, while considering uncertainties such as the hydrophones’ depth and the sound speed profile. The HMM is solved using dynamic programming for a batch localization solution. Region-of-interest (ROI) gating reduces the computational complexity towards real-time operation. Performance evaluation by emulations and a controlled sea experiment show that the proposed framework outperforms three reference methods in terms of localization accuracy, robustness to environmental uncertainty and computational efficiency. The implementation code is publicly available.
title: Dynamic programming-based range-depth estimation of sperm whale echolocation clicks using a two-element array

abstract: Distributed Acoustic Sensing (DAS) enables continuous monitoring of dynamic strain along tens of kilometres of optical fibre, generating massive datasets whose interpretation and automated analysis remain challenging. DAS data can be understood as a time-distance image array. However, the absence of standardised representation methods limits both the physical interpretability and the development of automated image-based analysis pipelines. This work introduces a systematic framework for visualisation and feature extraction of DAS data based on a multispectral signal representation. The approach decomposes strain-rate measurements into predefined frequency bands and produces band-limited energy images that describe the spatial and temporal distribution of acoustic energy across distinct spectral regimes. The framework is evaluated using DAS recordings containing fin whale and blue whale vocalisations. Three experiments are conducted to assess the approach: enhanced visualisation of bioacoustic signals, unsupervised clustering of acoustic patterns, and event detection using a convolutional neural network. The visualisation experiment shows that the multispectral representation allows for the simultaneous visualisation of sets of events that cannot be visualised using the strain amplitude representation. The unsupervised clustering experiment confirms that the multispectral representation yields class-discriminative feature spaces without requiring labelled data, enabling the automatic grouping of acoustically distinct event types. Finally, the use of multispectral composites as input of a ResNet-18 achieves an accuracy of 95.9% in whale vocalisation detection, demonstrating that the proposed representation provides an effective feature space for automated analysis. This approach provides a generalisable bridge between raw sensor data and standard computer vision pipelines, with implications for large-scale automated monitoring using fibre-optic sensor networks.
title: Multispectral representation of Distributed Acoustic Sensing data: A framework for physically interpretable feature extraction and visualisation

abstract: Domestic cats are known to be sensitive to human socio-emotional signals; however, how they process the emotional content of human vocalizations remains unclear. In this study, we investigated whether cats discriminate four basic human emotions (happiness, anger, fear, and sadness) expressed through non-verbal vocalizations, and whether these stimuli elicit lateralized auditory responses. Twenty domestic cats were tested in their home environment using a playback paradigm with human vocalizations. Behavioural responses were assessed through a composite score based on three stress-related behavioural categories (relaxed, moderate stress, and severe stress), together with head-turning direction, latency, and time spent looking at the speakers. Results revealed a significant effect of stress-related behavioural categories, with higher scores in the moderate stress condition compared to both relaxed and severe stress conditions, regardless of the emotional vocalization presented. In addition, no population-level asymmetries in head-turning responses were observed across emotional vocalizations. These findings indicate that human non-verbal vocalizations are sufficient to induce a measurable behavioural modulation in cats, but do not provide evidence of emotion-specific discrimination or lateralized processing at the population level. Instead, cats’ responses appear to reflect a generalized increase in arousal in response to human vocal cues, suggesting that vocal signals alone may convey limited information for fine-grained emotional decoding in this species.
title: Behavioural responses of domestic cats to human vocalizations reflect generalized arousal rather than emotion-specific processing

abstract: Cats experience stress during veterinary visits, though little is known about the association between cats’ personality traits and stress-related behaviours during these visits. This study aimed to identify personality traits in domestic cats using two methodologies to assess their ability to predict behaviours during a veterinary consultation. Twenty-nine healthy cats, ranging from 4 months to 10 years, were enrolled. Initially, cats underwent three behavioural tests: open field, novel object, and unfamiliar person. While the cats participated in the tests, the owners completed an adapted FE-BARQ questionnaire to assess fear, sociability, and aggressiveness. Subsequently, a simulated routine veterinary consultation was performed in two phases: anamnesis followed by the measurement of physiological parameters. The cat behaviour was recorded across all stages of the experiment. Principal component analysis extracted personality traits from the behavioural tests. To compare the traits extracted by the tests and owners’ responses with the cats’ behaviours during the clinical evaluation, linear regression models were used. A one-sided exact binomial test for paired proportions was used to assess whether predictive capacity differed between the tests and owners’ reports. Three personality traits were extracted and labelled as: attention-seeking, curious, and extroverted. Regarding the traits extracted through behavioural tests, during the anamnesis phase, more curious cats rested more (p = 0.03), hid less (p = 0.04), and displayed more threatening behaviour (p = 0.01). More extroverted cats displayed more play (p < 0.01) and scratching behaviours (p < 0.01). In contrast, traits reported by owners predicted these responses; the fear trait predicted more alert behaviour (p = 0.03), while the sociability trait predicted less alert behaviour (p = 0.01). During parameter measurement, more curious cats rested more (p = 0.04), rubbed more (p = 0.02), and displayed more threatening behaviour (p = 0.01), while more attention-seeking cats vocalised more (p = 0.03). In contrast, the fear trait reported by owners predicted less vocalisation (p = 0.04) during this phase. These findings indicate that, whilst both assessment methods could predict certain behaviours during the consultation, the behavioural tests identified a broader range of associations with clinical behaviours compared to owner reports. As an initial exploration into cat personality within veterinary settings, this study highlights the potential of using personality traits to refine individual handling and enhance assessments in veterinary practice to improve cat welfare.
title: The association between cat personality traits and behavioural responses during veterinary consultations
