abstract: This study presents a non-invasive acoustic monitoring framework for commercial pig fattening barns. It works in two steps: Model I separates pig (Sus scrofa) vocalizations from barn noise, and Model II classifies the retained calls as alarming or not alarming. Both models adapt the BEATs audio transformer to one-second clips in two phases. In Phase 1 , only a classifier head is trained on labeled data while the encoder stays frozen. In Phase 2 , the whole network is fine-tuned, and confident, class-balanced pseudo-labels from unlabeled recordings are added to the labeled data. In five-fold cross-validation, Phase 2 raised accuracy from 93.0% to 96.5% for pig detection and from 88.0% to 94.9% for alarming calls. On a held-out test set, the models reached 95.7% and 94.5%, outperforming MFCC-based classifiers and a fine-tuned HuBERT model. On recording months not seen during training, accuracy fell to about 85% (Model I) and 87% (Model II), and models trained on only one data source (farm or public) did not transfer to the other. An ablation attributed most of the Phase 2 gain to fine-tuning the encoder rather than to the pseudo-labels. In a retrospective assessment of 15 automatically flagged events, two veterinarians confirmed 60.0% and 73.3% as alarming, respectively. Agreement between the veterinarians was 81.8% on the 11 events assessed by both, with a Cohen’s kappa of 0.42. The framework is therefore proposed as an offline-validated, clip-level decision-support tool that directs expert attention to flagged periods, not as a real-time alerting system.
title: Semi-supervised audio transformers for non-invasive welfare monitoring in pig farming: a BEATs-based approach

abstract: Birdsong in oscine passerines is socially learned, but the relative influence of different tutors in the wild remains unclear for many species. We examined song acquisition in the Tree Pipit ( Anthus trivialis : Motacillidae), a migratory passerine with critical-period learning and temporally…
title: Like father, like son? Similarity of syllable repertoires and structures in the songs of first-year male Tree Pipits and their potential tutors

abstract: Eavesdropping on heterospecific alarm signals provides critical predator information, yet whether recognition is driven by innate phylogenetic biases or learning and ecology remains unclear. We hypothesize that decoding strategies arise from interactions between evolutionarily inherited perceptual biases and current ecological adaptations. To test this, we chose Asian Tits ( Parus cinereus minor ) as an “information hub species”, along with the Green-backed Tits ( P. monticolus ) and the Coal Tits ( Periparus ater ), forming a phylogenetic gradient. Playbacks used three call types: territorial song, ground alarm calls (hereafter “alarms”), and aerial alarms. Results demonstrated that Asian Tits exhibited a strong conspecific bias exclusively for ground alarms: fleeing probability in response to conspecific ground alarms (79.3%) was significantly higher than to heterospecific ground alarms, with no difference between the two heterospecific sources. Coal Tits were 2.89 times more likely to flee than Green-backed Tits in response to Asian Tit calls. These results support a binary conspecific-heterospecific distinction for ground threats, not a phylogenetic gradient. Decoding is call-type-specific: ground alarms elicit accuracy-driven responses, whereas aerial alarms permit more permissive decoding. Thus, heterospecific alarm decoding is shaped by signal function, a clear conspecific dichotomy and ecological niche, not by fine-scale phylogenetic distance.
title: Inherited biases reveal call-type-specific conspecific alarm responses in tits

abstract: While automated bioacoustic species classifiers play a growing role in avian population monitoring, they can produce false positive misclassifications by conflating acoustically similar sounds, including mimetic birdsong. We quantify the impact of the mimetic song of Northern Mockingbird ( Mimus polyglottos ) on the performance of BirdNET, a popular automated avian species classifier, and find that false positive detections caused by mimetic vocalizations persist in BirdNET results following common filtering methods, are indicated by detections of the mimicking species, and have an overall impact that varies with the focal species and the purpose of the bioacoustic survey. Of the 506 BirdNET false positives caused by Northern Mockingbird song in 22,483 BirdNET detections across 42 h of soundscape audio, 18 passed through species-based and confidence-based output filters. While mockingbird-associated false positives did not materially affect species richness patterns in our BirdNET results, they could impact detection rates or occupancy estimates, especially for some species. Though a case study with limited generalizability, our investigation shows that mimetic birdsong can affect the performance of this globally important avian passive acoustic monitoring tool. This impact may be explored by further study of BirdNET’s response to mimetic song and continued development of output filtering mechanisms.
title: Mimetic birdsong affects automated bioacoustic species classification: A case study using the Northern Mockingbird, a ubiquitous North American mimic

abstract: Vocal production learning is known to occur in a limited number of non-human taxa. Among birds, songbirds such as Zebra Finches ( Taeniopygia guttata ) are often studied as closed-ended learners, acquiring their vocal repertoire only during an early sensitive period, whereas open-ended learners like parrots can acquire new vocalizations throughout life. However, relatively little attention was paid to learning process of open-ended learners at different developmental stages. Whether open-ended learners such as Budgerigars ( Melopsittacus undulatus ) maintain high-level vocal learning ability into adulthood remains underexplored. Here, we investigated age-related differences in vocal learning capacity in Budgerigars by comparing their ability to learn human speech sounds at different ages. We found that the capacity to learn human vocalizations was retained into early adulthood. However, compared with juveniles, young adults showed a lower probability of successful learning and reduced overall imitation similarity within the training period. Interestingly, young adults exhibited significantly higher temporal order similarity in vocal output than juveniles. Nevertheless, birds aged 3–4 years old were unable to learn human speech sounds. These findings revealed that while Budgerigars are open-ended learners, their vocal learning ability declined with age. These results provide experimental evidence for understanding open-ended vocal learning and its changes at different developmental stages, and offer insights for comparative studies of human speech learning.
title: Vocal learning in juvenile and adult Budgerigars

abstract: The breeding distribution of Pallas’s Reed Bunting ( Emberiza pallasi ) extends from the Ural Mountains east to northeastern Siberia, with an isolated population ranging from southern Siberia to northern Mongolia. The species is generally regarded as polytypic, although the number of recognized subspecies varies from three to four depending on the author. Of these, E. p. lydiae is usually described as the most distinctive. To clarify the taxonomic status of this taxon, we analysed multiple independent datasets on mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA), genome-wide introns, morphometrics, and vocalizations. We also report the results of playback experiments and describe the geographical distribution and habitat preferences within the E. pallasi complex. Our results consistently support the existence of two evolutionarily distinct lineages. The first one corresponds to E. p. lydiae , which is associated with lowland steppe habitats in Mongolia and neighbouring parts of Russia and China, whereas the second includes E. p. pallasi , E. p. polaris and E. p. minor , which occupy higher-altitude shrubland environments, both within the geographical area occupied by E. p. lydiae ( E. p. pallasi ) and in Siberia ( E. p. polaris and E. p. minor ). Divergence between these two lineages is estimated to have occurred in the Middle Pleistocene. Within a modern biological species concept framework, these results support treating the subspecies lydiae as a distinct monotypic species, E. lydiae . We propose the vernacular names Mongolian Reed Bunting for E. lydiae and Siberian Reed Bunting for E. pallasi . We also provide a summary of integrative taxonomic studies of birds.
title: Taxonomy of Pallas’s Reed Bunting (Emberiza pallasi): An integrative approach

abstract: Functionally referential alarm calls convey predator-specific information, yet their ontogeny is contested. We hypothesized that nestlings possess an innate threat-detection system discriminating alarm calls from territorial songs but not fine subtypes or caller species. Their escape strategies (crouching down vs. jumping out the nest) are decoupled from perception and modulated by cavity-nesting tit species identity and local adaptation. Playback experiments on three cavity-nesting tits (the Asian Tit Parus cinereus minor , Green-backed Tit P. monticolus , and Coal Tit Periparus ater ) tested responses to conspecific/heterospecific ground and aerial alarm calls and territorial songs. Results showed geographic plasticity overrode fine discrimination in Asian Tit nestlings. All three species distinguished alarm calls from songs but showed no fine-scale discrimination by alarm type or stimulus source. Coal and Green-backed Tits exhibited conserved conspecific responses, failing to differentiate alarm calls (ground vs. aerial) or trigger jumping. However, heterospecific ground alarm calls triggered strategic divergence: Coal Tits jumped out of the nest (14.3%), whereas Green-backed Tits crouched down (0% jumping out). This suggests escape outputs are decoupled from perception, and point to a hierarchical ontogeny of anti-predator defense within cavity-nesting tits: geographic divergence, functional generalization, and species-specific strategic divergence, supporting the functional equivalence hypothesis.
title: Conserved perception and divergent action shape hierarchical anti-predator development in tits

abstract: The ultrasonic vocalizations (USVs) of house mice (Mus musculus) have a surprisingly complex structure and have been actively studied as a model for applied questions in biomedical science. Despite this, the functional significance of different USV types and their use during natural social behaviour in diverse groups remains unclear. In this pilot long-term study, we examined the ultrasound activity of female mice housed in stable groups within an enriched environment, focusing on how behavioural context influences USV time-frequency characteristics, call type occurrence, and nonlinear phenomena. Our findings show that USVs are mainly produced in bouts, and bouts containing ten or more variable calls always accompanying direct social interactions. USV variables and types varied markedly depending on the interaction context. During aggressive encounters, USVs and entire bouts became longer, vocalization time and frequency modulation increased, while peak and minimum fundamental frequencies decreased. Additionally, aggressive context was characterized by a higher prevalence of multi-component and complex-low USVs (with peak frequency < 50 kHz), and increased nonlinear phenomena. These results suggest that USV features closely reflect emotional arousal (intensity) and probably also valence (positive/negative) in female mice during social hierarchy formation and maintenance. Notably, the relationship between arousal and nonlinear vocal phenomena in mice USVs follows patterns observed in audible vocalizations of other mammals (increase with arousal). In the future, complex-low USVs could potentially serve as non-invasive indicators of negative emotional expression in groups of female mice. This opens new possibilities for acoustic home-cage monitoring aimed at welfare assessment and other applied uses.
title: Female mice in established social groups use different ultrasonic vocalizations during peaceful and aggressive interactions.

abstract: For many species, vocal communication is an essential part of mate selection and courtship. In songbirds, such as zebra finches (Taeniopygia guttata), a male's song can reveal much about his physiology and potentially even his developmental history, influencing female mate choice. It is thought that female zebra finches possess an auditory 'template' - potentially represented in the caudomedial nidopallium (NCM), caudomedial mesopallium (CMM), and/or caudocentral nidopallium (NCC) - that provides a standard for high- and low-quality song and guides behavioral preference. To investigate how finely tuned this template is to subtle differences in song, we employed an operant conditioning paradigm, using normal conspecific songs and Parkinsonian-like songs, which were derived from males overexpressing the human alpha-synuclein gene in Area X of the song circuit. Additionally, females were exposed to playbacks of these songs for immunohistochemical analysis of Zenk and c-Fos - protein products of the immediate early genes (IEGs) zenk and c-fos, respectively - in the NCM, CMM, and NCC. While the behavioral preference for either song type was inconsistent between females, females exposed to normal song exhibited significantly higher expression of both IEGs as compared to females exposed to Parkinsonian-like song in the NCC, but not in the NCM or CMM. These results suggest that the NCC may serve as a neural detector of subtle differences in song quality, while the NCM and CMM may influence preference behavior more directly.
title: A multisensory integrative forebrain area (NCC) in female zebra finches discriminates between normal and abnormal conspecific song

abstract: CpG oligodeoxynucleotides activate Toll-like receptor 9 (TLR9) and are used as vaccine adjuvants and immunotherapies, but their in vivo effects on the B-cell receptor (BCR) repertoire are incompletely defined. We administered the TLR9 agonist IMO-2125 to Indian rhesus macaques and African green monkeys and profiled peripheral-blood BCR repertoires at baseline, 24 h, 72 h, and 1 week. Light-chain clonotype and lineage diversity decreased after dosing, with the strongest lineage redistribution at 72 h. Most affected lineages decreased in frequency or clonotype number while showing increased mutation rates. Enriched heavy-chain lineages were biased toward mutated IgA and IgG and were consistent with memory- and effector-like B cells. The heavy-chain repertoire was comparatively stable, and responses differed in magnitude between species. These findings indicate that IMO-2125 rapidly reshapes the circulating BCR repertoire, most plausibly through selective redistribution of antigen-experienced B cells rather than broad clonal expansion.
title: Toll-like receptor 9 agonist IMO-2125 rapidly reshapes the B-cell receptor repertoire in non-human primates

abstract: Background The ciliary muscle is an important intraocular smooth muscle involved in accommodation and anterior segment physiology. RhoA/ROCK signaling regulates smooth muscle contraction and extracellular matrix (ECM) remodeling, but its involvement in ciliary muscle responses to hypoxia-like stress remains unclear. This study investigated the effects of CoCl 2 -induced hypoxia-like stress on guinea pig ciliary muscle cells (GCMCs) and the potential involvement of RhoA/ROCK-related signaling. Methods GCMCs were exposed to CoCl 2 to establish an in vitro hypoxia-like stress model. Cell viability was assessed to determine the appropriate concentration and exposure duration. Cells were divided into control, CoCl 2 , Y-27632, and CoCl 2 + Y-27632 groups. HIF-1α, RhoA, ROCK2, MYL9, phosphorylated MYL9 (p-MYL9), MMP2, and TIMP2 were analyzed by Western blotting, while RhoA, ROCK2, MMP2, and TIMP2 mRNA levels were assessed by RT-qPCR analysis. Reactive oxygen species (ROS), mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm), and intracellular Ca 2+ levels were evaluated by flow cytometry and fluorescence microscopy. A three-dimensional type I collagen gel contraction assay was used to assess cellular contractility. Both flow cytometry and fluorescence microscopy showed consistent patterns for ROS, ΔΨm, and intracellular Ca 2+ changes. Y-27632 (10 μM) was administered simultaneously with CoCl 2 and maintained throughout the 48 h treatment period to examine the contribution of ROCK-associated signaling to the observed responses. Results Treatment with 140 μM CoCl 2 for 48 h reduced GCMC viability to approximately 49% and significantly increased HIF-1α protein expression (P 2 significantly increased ROS and intracellular Ca 2+ levels and decreased ΔΨm (P 2 also increased RhoA and ROCK2 expression at both the protein and mRNA levels, accompanied by increased MYL9 and p-MYL9 protein expression (P 2 -induced changes in ROS, ΔΨm, intracellular Ca 2+ , RhoA, ROCK2, p-MYL9, MMP2, MMP2/TIMP2 ratio, and collagen gel contraction (P Conclusions CoCl 2 -induced hypoxia-like stress was associated with increased HIF-1α expression, oxidative and mitochondrial stress, altered intracellular Ca 2+ homeostasis, RhoA/ROCK-related signaling, enhanced contractility, and changes related to ECM remodeling-related changes in GCMCs. Partial attenuation by Y-27632 supports a contributory role of ROCK-associated signaling in these cellular responses.These findings provide a cellular basis for further investigating the relationship between hypoxia-like stress, ciliary muscle contractility, and ECM remodeling.
title: Involvement of RhoA/ROCK signaling in CoCl2-induced contraction and ECM remodeling in ciliary muscle cells

abstract: Irreversible cisplatin-induced hearing loss (CIHL) is a refractory chemotherapy-related adverse effect with limited clinical treatments. Schisantherin B (STB), a lignan isolated from Schisandra chinensis, is widely recognized for its neuroprotective properties, while its role in auditory injury remains unclear. Herein, we found that STB alleviated cisplatin-induced ototoxicity in House Ear Institute Organ of Corti 1 (HEI-OC1) cells and guinea pig models, protecting cochlear hair cells, synaptic ribbons and spiral ganglion neurons, and partially restoring auditory brainstem response (ABR) thresholds. Furthermore, combined drug affinity responsive target stability (DARTS) assay, the cellular thermal shift assay (CETSA), and the surface plasmon resonance (SPR) assay, we confirmed STB directly binds to the canopy FGF signaling regulator 2 (CNPY2), a key initiator of endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress. Notably, consistent dual in vitro and in vivo validation confirmed that STB exerts no regulatory effect on CNPY2 protein abundance, yet suppressed the downstream Protein kinase R-like endoplasmic reticulum kinase / C/EBP homologous protein (PERK/CHOP) signaling cascade and ER stress-mediated apoptosis. Moreover, molecular docking and co-immunoprecipitation (co-IP) validated the physical binding of STB to CNPY2 and the endogenous interaction between CNPY2 and PERK. Additionally, CNPY2 overexpression and shRNA knockdown further verified this functional relationship. Integrated proteomic and transcriptomic analyses showed STB partially reversed cisplatin-triggered inflammation and excessive ER stress. Collectively, our results suggest STB may serve as a potential otoprotective agent. The CNPY2-PERK/CHOP axis is closely linked to cisplatin-induced cochlear damage and offers a feasible target for intervention against CIHL. title: Schisantherin B mitigates cisplatin-induced ototoxicity by modulating the CNPY2-PERK/CHOP signaling axis

abstract: Like other pinnipeds, walruses Odobenus rosmarus produce aerial and underwater sounds to communicate with conspecifics. Although the acoustic displays, or songs, of wild breeding males in late winter remain one of the best studied aspects of walrus underwater vocal communication, little is known about their underwater calling during the non-breeding season. In July 2022, we obtained 233 h of underwater audio recordings of male walruses hauled out on Matveev Island in the southeastern Barents Sea (Pechora Sea) and found all main call types described for walruses from other Arctic regions, namely knocks, strums, bells, grunts, and whistles. Knocks and strums were produced in sequences with an average repetition rate of 2.9 and 1.5 per second, respectively, and appeared to be patterned. Codas, the most distinctive knocking pattern known from previous studies, were permanently present among the vocalizations of Matveev Island walruses, making them structurally similar to the coda songs emitted by Canadian walruses during the breeding season. The intensity of knocking and strumming varied during the 11-day study period reaching up to 134 signals/min but showed no clear diurnal variations. Our findings provide additional data on the seasonality and possible functions of the underwater vocal behavior of male walruses, supporting the idea that social learning and vocal practicing may play a role in the acquisition of their mating acoustic display.
title: Summer underwater vocalizations of male Atlantic walruses Odobenus rosmarus rosmarus near their terrestrial haul-out site.

abstract: Recent studies on the socio-cognitive abilities of animals, including elephants, have highlighted their aptitude to perceive and respond to human cues, particularly in captive settings. These abilities are crucial for fostering positive interspecies relationships and improving animal welfare in zoos. Previous research has shown that Asian elephants (Elephas maximus) can distinguish between familiar and unfamiliar humans through various sensory cues, such as visual and olfactory signals. Additionally, familiarity with caregivers reduces elephants' stress and has been linked to more cooperative behaviour and better task performance, highlighting its importance for the management and welfare of animals under human care. Yet the role of vocal communication in shaping these effects remains poorly understood, and less is known about how the type of speech caregivers use might affect elephants' behaviour. In the present study, we investigated how captive Asian elephants react to keepers' voices, focusing on the effects of voice familiarity, speech type and the interaction between the two variables on their behavioural response. We played recorded stimuli of familiar and unfamiliar voices speaking in either Elephant-Directed Speech (EDS), characterised by a high pitch and varied intonation, or Adult-Directed Speech (ADS), which does not present these acoustic characteristics. Our data show that vocal stimuli of any kind increased elephant arousal. Moreover, the elephants turned their bodies towards the doors used by the keepers - which we interpreted as behaviour indicative of a search for the keeper - when listening to EDS compared to ADS, or when the voice was uttered by a familiar rather than an unfamiliar keeper. However, no significant differences were found for the interaction between the speech type and familiarity for the duration of any behaviour analysed. Additionally, elephants engaged in aggressive displays more rapidly in response to ADS than to EDS, and initiated search-for-keeper behaviour significantly faster when exposed to EDS from a familiar keeper compared to EDS from an unfamiliar keeper. Overall, our results suggest that elephants can distinguish between familiar and unfamiliar voices and between two types of speech register with different acoustic features and therefore respond differently. Our work opens a window on the cognitive skills of the elephants.
title: Are you talking to me? Captive Asian elephants react to voice familiarity and Elephant-Directed speech

abstract: Voluntary vocal control is a fundamental component underlying vocal learning in animals. However, quantitative reports on the establishment of voluntary vocal control during training have been limited. In this study, we experimentally examined the trainability of voluntary vocal control in an aged male Pacific white-sided dolphin via operant conditioning with differential reinforcement of vocal responses. The dolphin was trained to suppress vocalizations during a standby condition and to selectively produce two call types (burst and chorus) in response to two distinct visual cues. Importantly, the learning process of the chorus, which the dolphin had not previously been trained to produce in response to cues, was evaluated. The learning criterion was reached after 30 training days and 42 sessions over a 126-day period, corresponding to approximately 1.5-2.5 h of systematic training. Results from the test phase demonstrated that the individual could voluntarily produce specific call types or suppress vocalizations in response to visual cues. These findings provide quantitative evidence of voluntary vocal control, a fundamental component of vocal usage learning, in an aged Pacific white-sided dolphin.
title: Experimental evidence for voluntary vocal control in an aged Pacific white-sided dolphin

abstract: Birdsongs are classified into two types based on behavioral context: undirected song (US) and directed song (DS). Comparisons of US and DS following manipulations of auditory feedback have provided insights into the mechanisms underlying adult song plasticity and maintenance. When deafened as adults, the US of the Bengalese finch changes more rapidly than that of other species (e.g., zebra finch and budgerigar). However, it remains unclear whether the DS of Bengalese finches undergoes similarly rapid degradation. In this study, we deprived adult male Bengalese finches of auditory input and conducted long-term comparisons of US and DS following deafening. We examined the ratios of the number of higher syllables to that of low syllables (H/L) to characterize both US and DS at each time point before and after deafening. After deafening, the decrease in H/L emerged significantly faster and greater in US than in DS. The syllable sequence stereotypy score was lower in US than in DS at 7-14 days after deafening. These findings demonstrate that in adult Bengalese finches, auditory deprivation induces greater alteration more rapidly in US than in DS. We discuss the possibility that differences between US and DS arise from distinct neural activity patterns in the anterior forebrain pathway, which is involved in song learning and modification.
title: Song modulation and auditory feedback under different behavioral contexts in adult male Bengalese finches

abstract: Like mammals, some reptiles possess sensitive and frequency-selective hearing at mid-to high-kilohertz frequencies. Both groups employ a place-frequency map within the inner ear to encode sound stimuli, but the mechanisms by which they achieve tuned nerve activation along the cochlea are believed to be distinct. To investigate the mechanical origins of auditory sensation in the reptiles, we measured sound-evoked displacement responses in the hearing organ of the tokay gecko (Gekko gecko), known as the basilar papilla. Using optical coherence tomography, we were able to resolve sub-nanometer-scale vibrations throughout the organ both in vivo and ex vivo. We saw that tuning was not present in the tissue-scale mechanics at any position within the organ; it instead exhibits an untuned rotational motion. We developed a mathematical model that predicted that this motion induces hair-bundle-stimulating fluid displacement and is due to an anatomical asymmetry seen in many reptile species. These results are consistent with the theory that hair-bundle-level mechanics are primarily responsible for tuning in the tokay gecko cochlea, and we argue that our proposed mechanisms generalize to many other species across the Reptilia class.
title: Rocking without a tune: Ex vivo and in vivo responses to sound in the basilar papilla of the tokay gecko

abstract: This paper evaluates the final major research effort of Hermann J. Muller, Nobel Laureate, to assess whether radiation displays a dose-rate process for radiation-induced germ cell mutation. Muller tried to extend the dose-rate findings of William Russell, Oak Ridge National Labs (ORNL), in male/female mice with his Drosophila fruit fly model. The paper reveals that Muller had no success in clarifying the dose-rate question with five years of substantial funding from the US Atomic Energy Commission (AEC). Despite a prolific scientific publication career, Muller published no data-based research articles in this area despite massive efforts, while Russell was publishing dose-rate discoveries with mice. This paper assesses the scientific reasons for Muller's failure to develop reliable information on the dose-rate issue in Drosophila, an area now well characterized by multiple research teams. The paper describes Muller's research strategies, how he coped with failure, research uncertainty and funding agency concerns with his lack of progress, despite his status. The paper shows that a frustrated Muller blamed the lack of success on erroneous dosimetry provided by physicists at Brookhaven National Laboratory, an argument that was refuted even to the satisfaction of Muller's staff. Yet Muller would alter the research record with respect to confirmation of the accuracy of the physicist's dosimetry, leading to the assertion that Muller's final research actions involved research misconduct via falsification. Muller's career at the University of Indiana would end in a frustrating manner for both the sponsor (AEC) and Muller and, with a new accusation of research misconduct.
title: Hermann J. Muller's research swan song: His long-term radiation dose-rate mutation investigations yielded no research publications, leaving questions of scientific misconduct

abstract: Dibutyl phthalate (DBP) and dibutyl adipate (DBA) are commonly used plasticizers that may pose risks to aquatic organisms. This study investigated whether DBP and DBA disrupt larval growth through neuroendocrine pathways using zebrafish (Danio rerio) as an in vivo model. Embryos were continuously exposed to DBP or DBA for 96 h, and growth-related morphological, transcriptional, and protein-level endpoints were assessed. DBP significantly reduced larval body length and increased locomotor activity, accompanied by decreased growth hormone (GH), insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1), and gamma-aminobutyric acid-A (GABA) receptor alpha 2 protein levels, as well as marked suppression of gh1, igf1, gad2, gabrb2, and gabrg2 expression. DBA produced qualitatively similar but consistently weaker effects, primarily affecting growth endpoints and selected neuroendocrine markers. Continuous co-exposure with the GABA A receptor antagonist bicuculline or the IGF-1 receptor inhibitor picropodophyllin did not further exacerbate growth inhibition or IGF signaling suppression compared with DBP or DBA exposure alone, revealing a non-additive interaction pattern. These findings suggest that DBP and DBA may impair larval growth through disruption of GABAergic and GH/IGF-related neuroendocrine regulation. Together, the results provide insight into the potential neuroendocrine mechanisms underlying plasticizer-induced developmental toxicity.
journal: Comparative Biochemistry and Physiology Part C Toxicology & Pharmacology
title: Disruption of GABAergic and GH/IGF-related signaling is associated with growth inhibition induced by dibutyl phthalate and dibutyl adipate in zebrafish

abstract: While many animals display behaviours resembling social conventions when interacting with conspecifics, it is unknown whether animals who live in close contact with humans develop sensitivity to our social conventions. With an eye-tracking study (N = 39), we asked whether dogs' (Canis familiaris) eye movements and pupil sizes would show a reaction when observing a violation in the customary response to human conventional communicative gestures ("come here" and "go away"). In the video stimuli, a human actress either approached or walked away from a second human actress. Both these actions (approaching or walking away) could be expected or surprising (within-subject), depending on whether they happened in response to the "come here" or the "go away" gesture of the second actress. While dogs' looking times and number of gaze transitions between the two actresses did not differ significantly between congruent and incongruent responses, their pupil size changes did: dogs' pupils dilated more when watching the incongruent responses (approaching after the "go away" gesture and walking away after the "come here" gesture) compared to the congruent ones. We discuss the possibility that pet dogs, during their ontogeny, implicitly form expectations about the usual response to some conventional human gestures. These expectations are not self-centred, as they were evidenced when dogs observed a third-party interaction between two humans, and they are context-specific, as the same responses elicited surprise following one gesture but not the other. We also consider alternative explanations and limitations of our findings.
title: Pupil size changes reveal that dogs are sensitive to the social conventions behind human gestures

abstract: Monitoring deer behaviour continuously and objectively is essential for accurate welfare assessment in pastoral farming, yet conventional observation methods are labour-intensive and prone to subjective bias. We present an unsupervised machine-learning pipeline for classifying farmed red deer ( Cervus elaphus ) behaviour from wearable accelerometer data. Tri-axial accelerometers mounted on the head and ear of stags recorded movement at 50 Hz over 48 h. k -means clustering of the normalised signals yielded eight prototypical movements spanning three behavioural categories: inactive states (lying, resting with or without rumination/panting), grazing (stationary and walking), and rapid ear flicks. A first-order Markov chain then linked these prototypes into higher-order sequences we call ”super-prototypes”. These compound behaviours included ear-flick bouts and alternating grazing-stepping cycles. Within the single 24-h window, activity varied with time of day, ear flicks being markedly more frequent by day. Against independent video annotation, the eight categories agreed with the observer’s labelling at a mean of 0.96 across prototypes. Because classification reduces to a nearest-centroid operation, the algorithm runs on a 16 MHz microcontroller at over 4 × 1 0 8 classifications per second, four orders of magnitude faster than the sensor sampling rate. The pipeline requires no hand-labelled training data and runs in real time on the animal, a feasible basis for welfare monitoring in extensive deer farming systems once validated under field conditions.
title: Behavioural phenotyping in red deer: Machine learning classification of accelerometer data from micro-movements to grazing

abstract: For humans, being looked at directly can boost our readiness to follow another's gaze, but can monkeys invite an observer to engage with them in the same way? We trained three rhesus macaques on a head gaze-following task in which the portrait of a demonstrator monkey would face the viewer before turning to look at a distinct spatial target. The demonstrator could face the viewer with their eyes opened or closed and display different facial expressions. Unlike in humans, we found that direct gaze alone, devoid of an accompanying specific expression failed to influence the latency of the subsequent gaze-following response. However, when combined with threat, direct gaze significantly accelerated gaze-following. In a second experiment, we show that once turned away the expression associated with prior direct gaze no longer mattered; instead a submissive facial expression accompanying the gaze shift delayed gaze-following. Direct comparison of both experiments reveals that expressions accompanying direct gaze trigger earlier gaze-following responses than the same expressions joining gaze aversion. These results document the behavioral relevance of threat-related facial expressions for gaze-following in rhesus macaques, with expressions that signal conflict selectively expediting orienting responses.
title: Monkeys integrate facial expressions and direct gaze to modulate gaze-following behavior

abstract: Acoustic communication is widespread among animals, but only a small number of species develop their communication signals through learning.1 In most species, the production of acoustic signals is thought to be hard-wired. Male Drosophila melanogaster are born knowing how to perform their courtship songs,2,3 which comprise alternations of three syllable types (two "pulse" modes and one "sine" mode4). Although males do not learn their songs, their singing is highly flexible5: males adjust both pattern and amplitude relative to female feedback6,7 and internal state.8 We therefore asked whether males can change the mapping between social context and song production-a form of "usage learning" involving alteration of the context in which an innate signal is used.9,10 Social experience-dependent learning in male Drosophila has been studied mainly as associative suppression of courtship,11,12,13 leaving open whether males can adjust their courtship strategy. Such usage learning could optimize innate behaviors for novel circumstances and has been described in other animals.14,15,16 Here, we use closed-loop optogenetics to perturb female feedback and demonstrate that Drosophila melanogaster males that experience such perturbed feedback subsequently alter the context in which they sing with new females, enabling the dissection of the genetic, neural circuit, and evolutionary mechanisms of usage learning.
title: Recent social experience alters song behavior in Drosophila.

abstract: In sexually reproducing animals, accurate sex recognition is fundamental for successful mating. Bidirectional signals are a sexually selected mechanism of mate recognition 1 , involving different, sex-specific cues to signal identity and reduce recognition errors. However, when these signals are insufficiently divergent or become obscured by environmental noise, the probability of misidentification can increase dramatically 2 . Among frogs, same-sex sexual behavior is widespread and is frequently attributed to sex-recognition errors, ambiguous signals, male-biased sex ratios or the instinct to indiscriminately clasp (amplexus) any suitably sized object they encounter 3 . Commonly, the male that has been erroneously clasped will emit 'release calls' 4 . It has been unclear whether frogs have evolved specific mechanisms to avoid such mistakes during acoustic interactions. Here, we report evidence for an acoustic mechanism in concave-eared torrent frogs (Odorrana tormota), through which males reduce such amplexus errors.
title: Acoustic strategy for avoiding same-sex amplexus in male concave-eared torrent frogs

Moreover, large-scale perturbations used so far have prevented quantitative spatial characterization of compensation. Here, we use the Drosophila larval wing disc to study the impact of local induction of apoptosis on tissue size and proliferation pattern. We first confirmed that the wing could recover its final size despite mild induction of apoptosis. However, using spatial statistics, we surprisingly found that local induction of death is not associated with any local increase in proliferation. abstract: Alston's singing mouse has emerged as an intriguing model for the comparative study of vocal control. New work on the species sets the stage to understand the proximate mechanisms and evolutionary roots of novel acoustic communication traits.
title: Integrative neurobiology: Tracing the origins of vocal innovations

abstract: Understanding the function and origin of a complex animal display requires a holistic study of its performance. For example, movement is linked to sound production 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 by enhancing or biomechanically facilitating displays, 7 , 8 exploiting additional sensory channels, 9 , 10 or affecting signal development and perception. 1 , 11 , 12 Among animal displays, humpback whale (Megaptera novaeangliae) song is remarkable for its hierarchical structure, syntax, and cultural transmission, 13 , 14 , 15 , 16 , 17 , 18 , 19 but it has been challenging to study the whole performance. Using temporarily attached sound and movement recording tags, we conducted an individual-level examination of fine-scale movement during humpback whale song performance. We discovered a tight correspondence between dives and songs, which were repeated without stopping for up to 16 h. Repeating song elements, known as themes, were linked to specific parts of a dive; ascent and descent song themes were consistent across individuals and years, while a greater number of theme types occurred at depth. Different levels of variability in song components across dive phases suggest that features of themes from the bottom portion of a dive, where the depth is stable, are more likely to be driven by song sharing under sexual selection. Movement during song performance illustrates important connections between physiology, environment, and behavior for learned, rhythmic acoustic displays.
title: Humpback whales match song production to dive patterns

abstract: Animals exhibit sex-specific behaviors that are governed by sexually dimorphic circuits. One such behavior in male Drosophila melanogaster, courtship, is regulated by various sensory modalities, including olfaction. Here, we reveal how sexually dimorphic olfactory pathways in male flies converge onto lateral horn output neurons, third-order neurons in the olfactory circuit, to regulate courtship. To achieve this, we developed ds-Tango, a modified version of the monosynaptic tracing and manipulation tool trans-Tango. In ds-Tango, two distinct configurations of trans-Tango are positioned in series, thus providing selective genetic access not only to the monosynaptic partners of starter neurons but also to their disynaptic connections. Using ds-Tango, we identified a node of convergence for three sexually dimorphic olfactory pathways. Males in which this node is silenced aberrantly court other males, unless a female is present. Thus, our results identify lateral horn output neurons important for proper courtship behavior and establish ds-Tango as a tool for disynaptic circuit tracing.
title: Convergent olfactory circuits for courtship in Drosophila revealed by the circuit-tracing tool ds-Tango

Yet accumulating evidence suggests that this view is too coarse. We previously identified discrete, macro-scale, vocal subunits of ∼80 ms within the common marmoset phee call, revealed by noise-evoked cancellations 1 1. Am. 2015; 138 :2906-2928 Crossref Scopus (86) PubMed Google Scholar , we find that vocalizations are constructed from a shared pool of discrete, rhythmically organized vocal motor elements (VMEs) in the gamma range (30–90 Hz 4 ), shorter than vocal subunits in phee calls. VMEs follow a quantized logic: their durations and frequency slopes are conserved across call types, akin to a shared ‘alphabet’. We propose a modular motor architecture model in which marmoset vocalizations are governed by a hierarchically nested, rhythmically gated set of VMEs. This provides a missing link between peripheral biophysical constraints and vocal evolution, suggesting that the combinatorial foundations of human speech may have emerged from pre-existing, rhythmically gated motor modules.
title: Marmoset vocalizations are built from discrete vocal motor elements

abstract: BACKGROUND: Extracellular adenosine triphosphate (ATP) signalling via purinergic receptors plays a key role in cochlear adaptation to loud sound. Traditionally, ATP activation of purinergic receptor P2X receptors has been proposed to induce a cation shunt, reducing the endolymphatic potential and the driving force for sound transduction. However, direct evidence for this protective mechanism remains limited. Here, we provide direct experimental evidence identifying a distinct, compartment-specific ATP signalling pathway that modulates cochlear function. METHODS: In mature Dunkin-Hartley guinea pigs of either sex, we combined time-resolved confocal microscopy, electrophysiology, live-cell imaging, and fluorescence spectroscopy to characterise how compartmentalised extracellular ATP regulates cochlear function during moderate loud sound exposure. FINDINGS: ATP delivered to the perilymphatic space where P2X2 receptors localised in Reissner's membrane epithelial cells, supporting cells, and hair cells significantly reduced sound-evoked electrical potentials from 486 μV to 315 μV, outer hair cell stereocilia motion from 135 nm to 99 nm and Hensen's cell motion from 128 nm to 101 nm at 80 dB SPL. These effects were reversible upon ATP removal and accompanied by decreased intracellular calcium. In contrast, ATP applied to the endolymph produced no comparable changes. These findings demonstrate that extracellular ATP in the perilymph protects the cochlea from high-intensity sound through a mechanism distinct from the classical cation shunt model. INTERPRETATION: These findings reveal a previously unrecognised perilymph-driven ATP signalling pathway that extend beyond the traditional P2X-mediated cation shunt, demonstrating that extracellular ATP plays a critical role in protecting the cochlea mainly from loud sound-induced hearing loss. FUNDING: Swedish Research Council 2017-06092 and 2022-00548.
title: Perilymphatic ATP plays a critical role in modulating cochlear function to protect from loud sound induced hearing loss

abstract: Current approaches to detect roaring behaviour of lions ( Panthera leo ) within acceleration data are scarce and limited to males that are stationary. We propose a segmentation approach using a Fully Convolutional Neural Network (U-Net) that can also work with data from females and roars that happen while the lion is walking. We equipped seven lions with a GPS/accelerometer and an audio logger. We merged audio and acceleration data to identify roaring signals in the acceleration data. We then trained a U-Net to differentiate between “roaring” and “no roaring” data. As training data we used segments containing only “no roaring” data and segments with a mix of “roaring” and “no roaring”. Finally, we used our classifier on the complete data from five lions to test how well the classifier would perform when roaring events only make up a small portion of the data. Our model shows a precision for “roaring” data points of 0 . 94 ± 0 . 01 (mean ± 95 % confidence interval) and a recall of 0 . 73 ± 0 . 01 over all individuals. Based on this, we could correctly identify between 90% and 96% of all roaring bouts with a precision between 87% and 100%. We showed that our approach can detect lion roaring behaviour of males and females in a stationary and walking context reliably. This can broaden the context in which lion communication can be studied and thus provide less biased data.
title: Did U hear that? Working with mixed behaviours when classifying animal behaviour from acceleration data using a U-Net

abstract: The Cuban treefrog ( Osteopilus septentrionalis ), as an invasive species in the southern United States, presents a need for effective surveillance. Automated detection expedites processing of audio data for large-scale surveillance and monitoring programs. However, current available methods commonly used for anuran species have not been sufficient to detect Cuban treefrogs. Here, we present results from a two-stage method for automated detection that employs both cross-correlation template matching and secondary supervised learning classifiers. In the first stage, audio data are screened for initial detections using template matching, in which the detections contain both true and false positives. In the second stage, the false positives are screened out using classifier algorithms. We used this method to process 139,985 audio recordings, consisting of 596,046 total minutes, collected at 13 locations in Louisiana and Florida from 2014 to 2022. From the stage 1 template matching, we detected 83,191 Cuban treefrog signals across recordings. The stage 2 machine learning model was able to identify stage 1 false positive detections with a testing accuracy of 98.46% and a testing false positive rate of 1.116%. After pruning false positive detections, a total of 20,271 individual Cuban treefrog detections remained, distributed mainly across 3 sites in an area with known presence. Locations with presumed absence had an easily verifiable number of false positive detections ( n = 109 across all other sites). The two-stage methodology utilizing both template matching and machine learning algorithms can be integrated into wildlife surveillance or monitoring programs for species with distinctive, conserved calls as an effective way to achieve sensitive species detection with a low incidence of false positives.
title: Two-stage approach to automatic detection with machine learning for improved surveillance of the invasive Cuban treefrog

abstract: Research in bioacoustics, neuroscience, and linguistics often uses birdsong as a proxy to acquire knowledge across diverse areas. This requires audio models to annotate and parse the birdsong. Developing such models requires precise, syllable-level annotated training data. Therefore, automated methods that reduce annotation costs are in demand. This work presents a data-efficient birdsong annotator called Residual Multi-Layer Perceptron Recurrent Neural Network. It then presents a three-stage training pipeline for developing reliable birdsong syllable detectors with minimal annotation. The first stage is self-supervised learning from unlabeled data. Two of the most successful pretraining paradigms are explored, namely, masked prediction and online clustering. The second stage is supervised training with effective data augmentation to produce a robust frame-level syllable detector for each individual. The third stage is a semi-supervised post-training step that refines each individual’s model using unlabeled data. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated for the Canary song in extreme label-scarcity scenarios. From a signal-processing perspective, the Canary song exhibits one of the most challenging spectro-temporal patterns for algorithmic time-series annotation: rapid vocalizations, brief inter-syllabic intervals, fast and broadband frequency sweeps, and spectrally similar syllables that require fine-grained features to distinguish. Hence, a successful syllable detection algorithm for Canary also establishes a robust baseline for other birds. This methodological generalization is validated in a case study of Bengalese Finch song annotation. Finally, the potential of self-supervised embeddings is assessed for linear probing and unsupervised birdsong analysis.
title: Data-efficient self-supervised algorithms for fine-grained birdsong analysis

abstract: Shipping underwater radiated noise (S-URN) has been shown to harm whale populations, yet the mechanisms by which anthropogenic sounds interfere with whale vocalization systems are less understood. This paper investigates the impacts of S-URN on the structure of sperm whale coda vocalizations for hundreds of codas collected in the Eastern Caribbean. For the dataset collected, we show that the presence or absence of S-URN can be used to classify coda features, which arguably indicates a systematic effect on sperm whale vocalization. S-URN also results in changes in the spectral properties of the codas. In particular, S-URN decreases the accuracy of coda spectral classification even at short distances (several meters), suggesting that underwater noise impacts the structure of sperm whale coda signals. We further show that in the presence of S-URN, codas are shorter and more coda signals with a specific spectral pattern are vocalized.
title: Evidence for the influence of shipping underwater radiated noise on sperm whale coda structure

abstract: Quantifying received noise levels at georeferenced positions of free-ranging marine mammals requires the fusion of heterogeneous, high-resolution data streams from multiple sensor modalities — a challenge that has not been addressed. This study presents an ecological informatics framework that integrates drone-based aerial video, YOLO-based vessel detection, a custom geoconversion algorithm (GeoConvertor) for pixel-to-geographic coordinate transformation using flight telemetry, and concurrent passive acoustic monitoring to estimate vessel-specific acoustic source levels and spatially explicit noise exposure at georeferenced animal positions. The framework was deployed in a coastal dolphin-watching setting off Jeju Island, South Korea, processing 187 vessel passage tracks across four vessel categories and 471 annotated Indo-Pacific bottlenose dolphin ( Tursiops aduncus ) surfacing events over 11 observation days. The GeoConvertor achieved sub-metric frame-to-frame positional stability (mean error: 0.15 ± 0.08 m), with velocity estimation RMSE of 1.27–3.11 km/h (0.68–1.68 kt) for land-based targets across speeds of 15–35 km/h and 0.23–0.79 kt for maritime targets across speeds of 3–18 kt at 100 m operational altitude. Linear regression of drone-derived vessel speed against hydrophone-measured source levels revealed strongly vessel-category-dependent relationships, with slope coefficients ranging from 0.17 to 1.77 dB/kt across frequency bands overlapping the dolphin whistle range (5.3–12.5 kHz). Dolphin-centric spatial analysis and threshold exceedance mapping showed that small-sized boats exhibited the highest proportion of encounters exceeding the conservative 3 dB masking criterion (93%). In comparison, large-sized boats showed the high exceedance of the 6 dB threshold (25%) despite maintaining greater standoff distances, with vessel type — rather than proximity — emerging as the dominant predictor of noise exposure. The framework demonstrates how multi-sensor data fusion and deep learning-based object detection can generate ecologically actionable, spatially explicit noise exposure estimates at georeferenced animal surfacing positions that are inaccessible to any single monitoring modality and are potentially transferable to other cetacean tourism settings and vessels noise monitoring contexts.
title: Beyond approach distance: A drone–hydrophone integrated framework for quantifying vessel noise masking risk to free ranging wild dolphins

abstract: Birdsong performance traits offer a mechanistically grounded route for developing non-invasive indicators of avian physiological condition at ecologically relevant scales. Sexual selection and honest signalling theory predict that complex, energetically costly song traits should be condition-dependent and thus sensitive to stressors such as parasitism and physiological stress. However, it remains unclear whether these relationships scale beyond individuals or single species to the plot level that would matter for monitoring programs. Here, we explicitly frame birdsong traits as a candidate state indicator and ask whether variation in health metrics across forest plots is reflected in corresponding changes in performance-related acoustic traits. We combined blood-derived health metrics with passive acoustic recordings from 17 forest plots in south-west Germany, focusing on five common songbirds ( Erithacus rubecula , Fringilla coelebs , Parus major , Sylvia atricapilla , Turdus merula ). For each species-by-plot combination, we quantified median haemosporidian infection intensity and heterophil-to-lymphocyte ratio. We extracted performance-related song traits using automated acoustic metrics (peak frequency, spectral bandwidth, number of spectral peaks, chroma variance, tonnetz variance) from species-specific, BirdNET-based classifications. Using mixed-effects models at the species-by-plot scale, we tested whether variation in these health metrics correlates with acoustic feature expression. Across species, multiple acoustic traits responded to variation in infection intensity and immune activation, although the direction and magnitude of responses differed among taxa. Importantly, models including health metrics consistently outperformed species-only models, demonstrating that aggregated acoustic trait expression tracks aggregated physiological condition at the plot scale. Although response directions differed among species, models including health metrics consistently outperformed species-only models, demonstrating that health-acoustic relationships are systematic rather than random. These results suggest that acoustic indicators of avian health must be interpreted relative to species-specific baselines rather than assuming a universal response across taxa. Building on this evidence, we propose that performance-related song features serve as candidate indicators of avian physiological condition. Their non-invasive collection via passive acoustic monitoring and sensitivity to health variation make them promising components of scalable monitoring frameworks. Rather than presenting a finalised composite index, this study establishes the conceptual and analytical groundwork for developing health-linked acoustic indicators that complement traditional biodiversity metrics by adding functional information on organismal condition.
title: Towards a non-invasive bioacoustic indicator of avian health: Linking song performance traits to physiological condition

abstract: Passive Acoustic Monitoring (PAM) is increasingly used as a non-invasive tool for biodiversity monitoring, particularly for species breeding in habitats where visual surveys are difficult or biased. The Critically Endangered African Penguin ( Spheniscus demersus ) is a highly vocal, burrow-nesting colonial seabird, making it an ideal species for evaluating whether soundscape data can be translated into reliable estimates of nest density. We deployed Autonomous Recording Units at multiple sampling points at the Stony Point Penguin Colony, South Africa, over two consecutive breeding seasons (2024 and 2025), capturing soundscapes spanning different nest densities and environmental conditions. We developed an automated detector for Ecstatic Display Songs (EDS), the species' territorial song, using a Convolutional Neural Network trained on a multi-source dataset from both in situ and ex situ recordings. The detector achieved high recall and precision, supporting the use of heterogeneous training datasets for reliable detection. To link vocal activity to nest density, we derived, for each sampling point, an index based on the maximum number of EDS detections across 30-min recordings and modelled its relationship with active nest counts using Generalized Additive Models. The index reliably predicted nest density, but the relationship was nonlinear: nest density rose as vocal activity increased before plateauing at higher levels. The model trained on 2024 data generalized well to independent 2025 data. Together, these results show that, up to intermediate densities, nest density can be reliably estimated from passive acoustic recordings alone. This approach requires no observer presence and is applicable to large-scale, long-term seabird monitoring.
title: Acoustic remote sensing with deep learning enables non-invasive estimation of seabird nest density

abstract: Riparian forests are biodiversity hotspots, yet their structural complexity has long hindered systematic habitat monitoring. Until recently, the lack of integrated technologies limited the identification of priority conservation areas at fine spatial scales. We investigated the habitat suitability of P. viridis , a bioindicator of mature and structurally complex woodlands, in three riparian biotopes of South Tyrol (Italy). Acoustic occurrence data were obtained from AudioMoth recorders and processed with BirdNET to derive daily presence/absence observations. Environmental predictors included LiDAR-derived structural metrics, Sentinel-2 NDVI descriptors, and spectral heterogeneity metrics aggregated at 90 m resolution. We modelled daily acoustic occurrence using Partial Least Squares Regression (PLSR) and generated relative acoustic habitat suitability maps, assessing model robustness through leave-one-logger-out and leave-one-area-out validation frameworks. Local predictive performance varied among study areas, and suitability maps revealed spatial associations between predicted relative acoustic suitability and local forest-structure gradients. However, transferability among biotopes was limited, with marked declines in predictive performance when models were transferred across study areas. Predictor importance also varied substantially among riparian systems, suggesting strong local ecological context dependence. Logger level validation showed only limited agreement between observed and predicted occurrence rates, while between-area transferability was poor. This study shows that integrating passive acoustics and remote sensing can help characterize local patterns of relative acoustic habitat suitability, while also highlighting important limitations in transferring species distribution models across heterogeneous landscapes. These findings emphasize the need for caution when extrapolating acoustic SDMs beyond local calibration contexts.
title: “…and the forests will echo with laughter!”: Remote sensing and bioacoustic integration for assessing Picus viridis distribution in structurally heterogeneous riparian forests

abstract: Environmental monitoring increasingly relies on non-invasive, presence-only data, like passive acoustic monitoring (PAM), yet the field lacks standardized frameworks to quantify changes in species' occurrence patterns. This study introduces a reproducible methodological framework to translate qualitative presence-absence time series data into comparable quantitative indices using recurrence (re-detection probability within a defined temporal window), a magnitude of change metric quantifying interannual variation, and persistence (consecutive presence duration). To validate these metrics, acoustic presence patterns of four endangered baleen whale species were analyzed using a decadal (2014–2023) PAM dataset from 112 sites across the U.S. East Coast. These metrics quantified diverging ecological realities: dietary generalist fin whales ( Balaenoptera physalus ) exhibited highly consistent patterns (97% recurrence, average magnitude of change 30%, average persistence <5 days). Furthermore, this framework captured the right whale's known decoupling from historical habitats associated with declining prey availability. Sei ( Balaenoptera borealis ) and blue whales ( Balaenoptera musculus ) exhibited seasonally discrete recurrence (93%) that aligned with their known seasonal foraging and migratory strategies. By characterizing these trends across species with varying foraging strategies, this framework demonstrates how multi-species monitoring can function as an ecological indicator of broader ecosystem and trophic trends. While demonstrated here using acoustics, this approach is applicable to any long-term presence-only data stream, bridging the gap between high-resolution monitoring and the requirements of quantitative ecological indicators. (248 / 250 words)
title: A standardized framework for quantifying species occurrence, applied to passive acoustic monitoring of baleen whales
Passive acoustic monitoring reveals seasonal bottlenose dolphin (Tursiops truncatus) presence in coastal estuarine waters

abstract: Microcystin-LR (MC-LR) and polystyrene nanoplastics (PSNPs) are ubiquitous co-pollutants in freshwater systems known to individually impair feeding in aquatic organisms, yet their combined ecological risks are inadequately defined. Here, we demonstrated that MC-LR exposure induced feeding abnormalities in zebrafish Danio rerio, and this effect was severely aggravated by co-exposure with PSNPs. Mechanistic studies revealed that PSNPs acted as a carrier, markedly enhancing the bioaccumulation of MC-LR in intestinal tissues. This process initially disrupted gut microbiota structure (reduction in beneficial bacteria like Bacteroidetes and Cetobacterium) and tryptophan metabolism, leading to suppressed synthesis of intestinal serotonin (5-HT). The deficiency in gut-derived 5-HT, in turn, provoked peripheral metabolic disturbances (hypoglycemia and hyperlipidemia) and an imbalance of appetite-regulating hormones (ghrelin, cholecystokinin, peptide YY, and glucagon-like peptide). These peripheral signals converged to dysregulate key hypothalamic neuropeptides (agouti-related protein, pro-opiomelanocortin, neuropeptide Y, and orexin), ultimately contributing to abnormal feeding behavior. Our study elucidates a complete pathway along the microbiota-gut-brain axis and identifies reduced gut-derived 5-HT as the critical hub linking pollutant exposure to neurobehavioral deficits, offering a novel perspective for assessing the ecological risks of complex pollutants.
title: Intestinal serotonin signaling suppression: A novel mechanism for overfeeding exacerbation by nanoplastics and MC-LR in zebrafish

abstract: Myopic axial elongation is driven by scleral remodeling, yet the metabolic events linking scleral hypoxia to autophagy-associated remodeling remain incompletely defined. We examined whether HIF-1α-dependent glycolytic reprogramming and lactate-associated metabolic stress connect hypoxia to remodeling changes in human scleral fibroblasts (HSFs) and in a guinea pig model of form-deprivation myopia (FDM). RNA sequencing showed significant enrichment of HIF-1 signaling and glycolysis/gluconeogenesis in hypoxic HSFs. Hypoxia increased HIF-1α, HK2, PFKP, and LDHA expression and raised intracellular lactate levels. Inhibition of glycolysis with 2-deoxy-D-glucose (2DG) or pharmacologic inhibition of lactate production with oxamate attenuated hypoxia-associated autophagy and remodeling marker changes. HIF-1α inhibition with acriflavine or siRNA suppressed glycolytic activation and mitigated downstream marker changes. Exogenous lactate partly restored autophagy- and remodeling-associated phenotypes during glycolytic or HIF-1α inhibition without restoring upstream glycolytic enzyme expression. Additional CQ-based flux assays supported that hypoxia enhanced autophagic flux and that lactate further increased CQ-sensitive LC3B II accumulation under hypoxia. pH-controlled experiments showed that sodium lactate under pH-normalized conditions and HCl-mediated acidification produced partially overlapping downstream effects, whereas unadjusted Lactate produced the strongest response, supporting combined contributions from lactate-associated signaling and extracellular acidification. GNE-140, used as an LDH/lactate branch-focused inhibitor, attenuated downstream autophagy- and remodeling-associated changes without materially suppressing upstream glycolytic enzymes, and lactate add-back restored the downstream phenotype. In vivo, subconjunctival 2DG reduced myopic refractive shift, axial elongation, posterior scleral thinning, collagen disorganization, abnormal glycolysis/autophagy/ECM marker expression, and FDM-associated scleral lactate accumulation. These findings support a model in which hypoxia-driven HIF-1α-dependent glycolytic rewiring generates a lactate-enriched acidic microenvironment that contributes to autophagy-associated scleral remodeling in experimental myopia.
title: Hypoxia-driven HIF-1α-dependent glycolysis/lactate-associated signaling promotes autophagy-associated scleral remodeling in experimental myopia

abstract: Epilepsy is a chronic neurological condition that is often accompanied by psychiatric comorbidities, including anxiety and social dysfunction. Several animal models of epilepsy exist but they are costly, laborious, and ethically constrained. In this regard, zebrafish (Danio rerio) offer a promising alternative animal model. However, most epilepsy studies have focused on acute seizure models, and long-term paradigms addressing neurobehavioral comorbidities are still lacking in zebrafish. We earlier developed a chronic pentylenetetrazole (PTZ)-induced kindling model in adult zebrafish that showed cognitive deficits. In the present study, we extended the work by investigating psychiatric comorbidities and associated molecular alterations in the previously developed model. Adult zebrafish were repeatedly exposed to 1.25 mM concentration of PTZ until kindling followed by assessment of anxiety and social function deficits. In results, kindled fish showed altered exploration, increased dark preference, and reduced social engagement, indicative of heightened anxiety-like behavior and social deficits. At the molecular level, increased slc25a5 and reduced ppp3r1a, bdnf, vdac3, and prohibitin, as well as significant increase in phosphorylated CREB was observed. The results suggested impaired mitochondrial function and dysregulated synaptic plasticity contributing to the observed behavioral alterations. The current findings support the utility of the chronic PTZ zebrafish model for studying epilepsy-associated psychiatric comorbidities and suggest its potential as a cost-effective platform for mechanistic studies and preclinical therapeutic screening.
title: Modulation of CREB signaling contributes to anxiety-like phenotypes in a kindling model of adult zebrafish

abstract: Reliable estimates of fish stock size are a prerequisite for sustainable exploitation. Active acoustic methods are cost-effective and non-intrusive means of quantifying pelagic organisms, delivering data with high spatial and temporal resolution. Recent advances in broadband echosounders have substantially improved range resolution, enabling effective detection of individual fish and opening opportunities for echo-counting - an approach not possible with traditional continuous wave acoustics. These advances now make it feasible to study benthopelagic fish stocks, i.e. fish stocks that are found both in the water column and in close proximity to the seabed, using echo-counting. However, the lack of standardized procedures has so far hindered the inclusion of echo-counting surveys in stock assessments. Here, we present a comprehensive method for estimating the total stock size of Atlantic cod ( Gadus morhua ), a benthopelagic species, using echo-counting and modern acoustic instruments. We compare results from echo-counting with traditional echo-integration and with the ICES assessment of Atlantic cod in the Nuuk fjord system – a favourable test scenario for benthopelagic fisheries acoustics. All approaches yielded comparable results. Based on these findings, we recommend echo-counting for benthopelagic fish stocks, where single echoes can be reliably resolved (Sawada index is <0.04), supplemented with echo-integration in the high-density patches. The framework outlined here for collection, processing, and analysis of acoustic data provides a foundation for developing guidelines and a roadmap towards the inclusion of echo-counting into official stock assessment.
title: Towards the inclusion of broadband acoustic methods in the assessment of benthopelagic fish stocks
