In addition, each call type contained information about individuality and sex-class membership, but not about age or breeding status. These results suggest that the Locomotion and Pre-flight calls of greylag geese carry information reflecting multiple facets of caller identity, potentially allowing familiar conspecifics to characterise their interactants even at a distance and in acoustically rich contexts.
title: Vocal identity and information content in the flight initiation calls of greylag geese ( Anser anser )

abstract: Non-human primates have long been considered to show limited flexibility in their vocal production, with changes mainly due to maturational mechanisms. However, several studies suggest that emotional, contextual and social factors are likely to affect acoustic variability in non-human primates, although it is often difficult to untangle them. In this study, we investigated whether these factors influence the acoustic variability of high whinnies, the most frequent contact call of Geoffroy’s spider monkeys (Ateles geoffroyi). We used an acoustic similarity index for each pair of high whinnies and behavioural indicators of anxiety-like emotion, context and social relationships to examine intra- and inter-individual acoustic variability. We found that anxiety-like emotion explained some acoustic variability, whereas the time two monkeys spent together did not. The main factor influencing variability was the context of emission, with high whinnies being more similar during feeding at the inter-individual level. Overall, our findings indicate a vocal convergence at the group level during feeding, possibly to enhance tolerance in a risky context.
title: Factors influencing acoustic variability in the contact calls of wild Geoffroy’s spider monkeys

abstract: The identification of individuals from their vocalisations offers a non-invasive approach to population monitoring, but only if individual vocal signatures are distinct and stay stable over time. We tested whether territorial calls of Boobook owls could meet these requirements and support individual acoustic monitoring in eucalypt open-forest. Six acoustic features were measured in 208 calls from eight reference owls (21–30 calls per bird) and analysed using linear discriminant analysis (LDA). Leave-one-out cross-validation achieved 82.7% classification accuracy, with mean frequency and spectral entropy (Hf) showing the greatest potential for vocal individual discrimination. The trained model was then tested in a field application using recordings from 11 consecutive nights of passive acoustic monitoring at a single study site. We evaluated 22 bouts (sequences of repeated territorial calls) from owls of unknown identity using predefined assignment criteria. A local resident owl was repeatedly re-identified, and two other owls were detected, one previously recorded locally and the other at a neighbouring site. These findings show that these owl calls contain individually distinctive acoustic signatures with potential for longer-term population monitoring, supporting the integration of passive acoustic monitoring, acoustic analysis, and machine learning into conservation and management practices, with potential applications to other species.
title: Vocal identification and monitoring of individual Australian Boobook owls ( Ninox boobook )

abstract: In the context of a declining avian soundscape, this research investigates poetic mimicry as a species-specific method of sympoiesis, or making-with, the Eurasian jay. The work emerges at the intersection of queer ecologies, queer ecopoetics, animal and literary studies, and with the “chatty acorn-eater,” Garrulus glandarius. Like the jay’s skreek, the paper explores the ways queer voices – and my poetic voice – transgress categorisation, as well as normative temporalities. Through three specific examples, I propose “creeping after” as an interspecies method of troubling original/mimicked poetic voice. Leaning (uncomfortably) close into the unsettling pleasure of boundary dissolution, this research pries and pilfers into the creation of poems as “creepy doubles.” Creeping after offers a methodological approach that integrates sustained interspecies encounter with creative-critical practice. While developing particularly Garrulus methods, the research invites other practitioners to explore the potential of poetic making- (and riddling-) with another single species. Beyond ecopoetics, this work possesses – or is possessed by – questions of non-human minds and the disruption of language through interspecies encounters. Nodding to the thrilling-but-terrifying potential of our ecosystemic bodies and voices, “creeping after” highlights the productive instability of all supposedly authentic expression. As a generous, generative practice, hopping between the branches of disciplines, it issues an invitation to embrace birdwatching and tactical poetic performance as creepy methods.
title: CREEPING AFTER: jays, gays, and copycats

abstract: Forest-dwelling bats rely heavily on cavity-bearing trees, making them sensitive to silvicultural practices that modify stand structure and microhabitat availability. This study investigated roost selection and seasonal habitat use in a Hungarian oak (Quercus frainetto) forest in northwestern Türkiye using box-transect surveys, direct cavity inspections, full-spectrum acoustic monitoring, descriptive and exploratory analyses across Hungarian oak stand types. Potential roost structures (n = 378) were recorded exclusively in degraded and high-canopy mature oak stands, which contained the largest and most structurally complex trees. Microhabitat abundance differed significantly between these stand types (Mann – Whitney U, p = 0.028), with mature stands supporting higher structural availability. Fourteen active roosts belonging to Pipistrellus nathusii, P. pipistrellus, and Nyctalus noctula were confirmed during the autumn. Across all seasons, 11 bat species were acoustically detected, although no winter activity was recorded. Exploratory analyses indicated that bat acoustic activity duration varied seasonally, with activity peaking during the summer, particularly in younger and structurally open stands. By integrating roost observations with spatial fire-risk assessment and other disturbance layers, the study identifies mature oak stands as structurally important yet spatially vulnerable habitat components within the landscape. These findings underscore the need to retain cavity-bearing trees, incorporate pre-harvest roost assessments, and align silvicultural operations with seasonal patterns of bat activity. Overall, the study provides one of the first integrated assessments of roost availability, seasonal habitat use, and spatial risk exposure for bats in Türkiye’s oak forests, offering a practical framework for integrating bat conservation into forest management planning.
title: Roosting ecology and habitat use of bats across different stand types in a Hungarian oak forest in northwestern Türkiye

abstract: Contact calls made by a provisioning parent approaching the nest increase provisioning efficiency whether the calls are directed to offspring to elicit begging or to a brooding mate to coordinate parental care. Songbird nestlings are completely dependent on parents for care, as they hatch blind, helpless, and unable to thermoregulate. We studied how often parent European Starlings (Sturnus vulgaris) vocalized when approaching their nest boxes in Halifax, Nova Scotia, Canada. We recorded audio of seven early-season and four late-season broods across four nestling ages (days 2, 4, 11, and 13) to determine whether parents called when arriving at the nest box and whether the other parent was in the box. We predicted parents would call more often when nestlings were young (days 2 and 4) than when older (days 11 and 13), either to elicit begging by the blind nestlings or to alert their mate to exit the box. If calls were directed to nestlings, then we predicted that calling would be unrelated to whether the other parent was in the nest box. If calls were directed to their mate, we predicted that the provisioning parent would call more often when the other parent was in the nest box. As predicted, parents called significantly more often when nestlings were young (62% of visits on day 2, 36% on day 4) than when older (4% of visits on day 11, 4% of visits on day 13), although parents reduced their calling earlier (day 4) in late-season broods (50% of visits in early- and 17% in late-broods). Parents called on a higher proportion of visits when the other parent was in the nest (85% of 68 visits) than when they were not (17% of 877 visits). Our results suggest that the intended recipient of calls is the other parent rather than the nestlings. Flexible communication at the nest would be adaptive as parents can call when nestlings are young to increase parental coordination and provisioning efficiency, then stop calling when nestlings are older as it is no longer required and could be costly in terms of predation risk.
title: European Starling ( Sturnus vulgaris ) parents call less often as their nestlings age

abstract: Originally identified as a chromatin domain insulator binding protein, Drosophila melanogaster BEAF (Boundary Element-Associated Factor of 32 kDa) is predominantly associated with transcription start sites (TSSs) of housekeeping genes. It was previously shown that BEAF directly interacts with the transcription factor Serendipity-δ (Sry-δ). TSS-proximal BEAF can interact with distantly bound Sry-δ to activate a reporter gene. However, it is unknown if the ability of BEAF to communicate with transcription-associated factors from a distance is a common property. Here, we use yeast 2-hybrid assays to show that BEAF directly interacts with a variety of transcription-associated factors: both FACT subunits (Dre4 and SSRP), DREF, Rib, ROW, Map60, Apt, Wds, Cdk1, GFZF, and weakly with Adf1 and Kdm5. We further explored the interaction of BEAF with the histone chaperone FACT and transcription factors DREF, Rib, and ROW, including interrogating communication from a distance with a reporter gene assay and by analysis of S2 cell high-throughput chromosome conformation capture (Hi-C) data. When tagged with a VP16 activation domain, all five proteins activated RpS12 and yellow promoters cooperatively with adjacent, promoter-proximal BEAF. Only ROW and the FACT subunit SSRP communicated with BEAF from a distance, and only ROW exhibited long-range interaction with BEAF in Hi-C data. Our results provide evidence for three mechanisms by which promoter-proximal BEAF might facilitate gene activation. First, it might affect promoter chromatin accessibility by recruiting chromatin proteins like FACT. Second, consistent with the model of housekeeping gene regulation by promoter-proximal elements, BEAF might cooperate with adjacent interacting transcription factors for promoter activation. Third, a subset of interacting transcription factors, including ROW and Sry-δ, might interact with BEAF from a distance, modifying the traditional paradigm of local regulation of housekeeping genes.
title: Characterization of physical interactions between the Drosophila insulator binding protein BEAF and transcription-associated proteins
why: title names a species not in the atlas

abstract: Advertisement calls of individually marked male Xenopus laevis were recorded in a South African pond to test for individual vocal signatures and information content. In a blind playback test, human listeners recognised the calls of three out of four males across two consecutive breeding seasons (1993–1994) at above-chance levels, demonstrating stability of individual call characteristics. In a larger 1998 sample (64 calls from 18 males), discriminant analysis of 32 acoustic parameters correctly assigned 95.3% of calls to the correct individual. All 11 frequency parameters were strongly (negatively) correlated with body size, but none of the 16 temporal parameters. Slower click rates in the slow trill were associated with higher male body condition. These findings show that male X. laevis advertisement calls are individually distinctive and consistent over time, and that call frequency and rhythm provide reliable cues to the caller’s size and condition.
title: Individuality of the advertisement call in Xenopus laevis (Pipidae)
The Role of Song in a Secondary Contact Zone between Two Coastal White-Crowned Sparrow Subspecies

abstract: Abstract Passive Acoustic Monitoring (PAM) is widely used for marine mammal observation, but conventional monitoring systems typically require continuous high-power signal acquisition and processing, limiting long-term autonomous deployment. In this work, we present an Always-On Sperm-Whale Detector (AO-SWD) based on a neuromorphic and ultra-low-power processing pipeline combining a bio-inspired artificial cochlea with FPGA-based spiking neural network (SNN) inference. The proposed system uses a 16-channel ultra-low-power (ULP) cochlea implemented in 65 nm CMOS technology operating in the subthreshold regime. The cochlea converts underwater acoustic signals directly into asynchronous spike trains while consuming only 4 μW total power (250 nW/channel). The generated spike-based representation is processed using lightweight feedforward SNN architectures trained with snnTorch and optimized for FPGA deployment using the ModNEF framework. Several network architectures and temporal resolutions were evaluated to study the trade-off between detection accuracy, latency, and hardware complexity. The best software configuration, using a network architecture of 16 input channels, 128 hidden neurons, and 1 output neuron with 20 time steps, achieved 93.30% classification accuracy for sperm whale click detection. The corresponding FPGA implementation achieved 91.15% accuracy after hardware-aware optimization while maintaining real-time operation. The proposed architecture demonstrates the feasibility of combining ultra-low-power neuromorphic sensing with embedded spiking inference for energy-efficient underwater acoustic monitoring. These results highlight the potential of event-driven bio-inspired systems for long-duration autonomous ecological monitoring applications.
title: Always-on ultra-low-power neuromorphic pipeline for real-time sperm whale detection

abstract: Abstract Climate change is predicted to increase incidents of heat stress, which is known to impair cognitive performance. Associative learning, a highly conserved cognitive trait, is thought to underpin anti-predator behaviour, though direct empirical evidence is lacking from natural populations. If true, this would imply that environmental stressors, such as heat stress, may affect the ability of wild animals to respond to predators. However, the effect of heat stress on the link between associative learning and anti-predator behaviour has received limited empirical attention. Using wild Western Australian magpies (Gymnorhina tibicen dorsalis), we investigated 1) whether associative learning predicts anti-predator behaviour, and 2) whether this relationship is influenced by heat stress. We predicted that birds with better associative learning performance would respond more strongly to a simulated predator threat, but that this relationship would be significantly weakened by heat stress. Consistent with our first prediction, we found that individuals with higher associative learning performance were more responsive to the simulated predator threat. Contrary to our second prediction, heat stress did not disrupt the relationship between associative learning performance and vigilance. Rather, individuals with better associative learning produced more alarm calls and took longer to return to normal behaviour under heat stress. These findings provide some of the first empirical support for the hypothesized link between associative learning and anti-predator behaviour in a wild bird population. Furthermore, they suggest that associative learning may facilitate behavioural adaptation to challenging environmental conditions by enabling individuals to integrate cues such as temperature into context-appropriate anti-predator responses.
title: Heat stress impacts the relationship between cognition and anti-predator behaviour in wild magpies

abstract: Abstract Predation is a major source of nestling mortality for many songbird species. Parental investment theory predicts that parents should defend nests based on offspring survival and recruitment potential and weigh current investment in nest defense against costs to their own survival and future reproductive opportunities, which may vary across species and be constrained by other life-history traits. We explored the relationships between parental investment in nest defense behavior and offspring age, number, and quality in eastern bluebirds (Sialia sialis) and tree swallows (Tachycineta bicolor), 2 species that breed concurrently in the same habitats and exhibit similar nest defense behavior but differ in their within-season re-nesting potential. We observed diving, alarm calling, and beak snapping by parents in response to repeated human visits to the nest box from laying through fledging over 5 consecutive breeding seasons and also measured nestling weight and size to assess quality over the later 3 breeding seasons. Tree swallows invested more in nest defense than bluebirds, and both species increased defense investment as nests aged. However, we found no association between defense and nestling quality or brood size. We discuss these findings in light of predictions stemming from parental investment theory as well as several previously proposed alternative hypotheses and suggest that the relationships between parental defense and fitness benefits for parents may be more subtle and complex than initially outlined by parental investment theory's predictions.
title: Fighter–pilot parents: relationships of nest defense with species, nest stage, and brood quality

abstract: Abstract Male bees navigate complex tradeoffs between energy acquisition and reproductive signaling, yet their movement strategies remain understudied. Unlike workers that optimize foraging to support the colony, male bumblebees (Bombus terrestris) forage independently to collect nectar and deposit sex pheromones on selected plants. Using high-resolution 3D tracking in an indoor flight cage, we investigated how the spatial arrangement of nectar and scent-marking sites, along with nectar availability, influence male movement patterns. We manipulated the distribution of feeders (artificial flowers) and scent-marking locations (branches), and varied nectar delivery rates, to assess effects on foraging, scent-marking, and patrolling. Males responded strongly to spatial structure: in clumped arrays with evenly spaced resources, movements between consecutive visits were shorter and more localized, while in dispersed arrays with irregular spacing, transitions were longer and more variable. The combination of dispersed spacing and low nectar availability imposed the highest foraging demands, resulting in fewer feeding events and reduced total feeding time. Despite these increased costs, males maintained consistent investment in reproductive behaviors, suggesting a prioritization of mate-seeking over energy gain. Rather than reducing signaling, males adjusted their foraging strategy—favoring fewer but prolonged feeding bouts when nectar availability allowed. These findings reveal a unidirectional behavioral adjustment, in which foraging is modulated to sustain reproductive effort, and show how spatial resource structure and nectar availability together shape movement decisions in male pollinators.
title: Male bumblebees sustain mate-seeking by adjusting foraging to environmental conditions

abstract: Abstract Prey often assess predation risk using multiple sources of information that differ in immediacy and reliability. How prey differentially weight direct predator-associated cues and heterospecific alarm cues remains a central question in behavioral ecology. To investigate this, playback experiments were conducted on free-ranging, predator-experienced Southern giraffes (Giraffa giraffa), using lion (Panthera leo) vocalizations and red-billed oxpecker (Buphagus erythrorhynchus) alarm calls presented in different positions within sequential playback trials. Lion vocalizations consistently elicited strong vigilance responses regardless of playback presentation order, indicating that giraffes assigned greater behavioral weight to direct predator-associated information. Giraffes also responded to oxpecker alarm calls, although responses were generally weaker and more variable than responses to lion vocalizations, suggesting that indirect heterospecific cues were weighted less strongly than direct predator cues. Evidence that preceding playback exposure strongly influenced subsequent vigilance responses was limited, as lion vocalizations continued to elicit stronger responses than oxpecker alarm calls across successive playbacks. Females additionally exhibited generally stronger vigilance responses than males across playback conditions. Together, these findings suggest that giraffes differentially weight multiple sources of risk-related acoustic information during antipredator responses.
title: Differential weighting of lion vocalizations and oxpecker alarm calls in giraffes

abstract: Abstract Mobbing is a widespread antipredator strategy among prey species and can be considered as a form of cooperation. As such, it is expected to be enhanced when the perceived risk of predation is locally increased. Here, through a manipulation of the landscape of fear (variation in the perceived predation risk 3 min per day), we study how it affects the propensity to engage in mobbing behavior of 2 Paridae species (great tit and blue tit). For our 2 target species, a high perceived risk of predation led to a greater engagement in mobbing behavior. Additionally, we found no difference in mobbing engagement between the 2 species (even though the acoustic stimuli used were only heterospecific for the great tit), suggesting that heterospecific cooperation also increases when the risk of predation increases.
title: Perceived predation risk increases mobbing intensity in tits

abstract: Abstract Animals in dangerous situations often use alarm calls to warn others. Variation in this behaviour across different social settings can serve to answer long-standing questions about the evolution of costly cooperative actions, since warned conspecifics may yield kin-selected, reproductive or mutualistic benefits to the caller. We experimentally tested how responses to predators vary according to differences in social settings in wild Eurasian magpies (Pica pica). Magpies called more and approached predator models more closely when they were with their partner. This effect persisted in the non-breeding period when no offspring were present any more, suggesting that magpies engage in anti-predator behaviour to warn or protect their breeding partner as well as their offspring and thereby gain both future and current reproductive benefits. In contrast, the low alarm call rates of lone magpies or flocks suggest that self-serving pursuit-deterrent alarm calling, quality advertisement, kin selection, or immediate mutualistic benefits (help in defence) do not function as drivers of alarm calling in this species. Our approach enabled us to test the various hypotheses on the evolution of alarm calling in a year-round territorial bird species, and suggests that long-term benefits of partner maintenance can outweigh short-term costs of risky alarm-calling behaviour.
title: Social environment predicts alarm calling in Eurasian magpies

abstract: Abstract Chemical signals play a key role in intraspecific communication in many animal species, especially in reproductive contexts. However, these signals may entail costs if detected by predators. In anurans, studies on communication have traditionally focused on acoustic signals, while the use and function of chemical cues remain poorly explored, making it unknown whether these secretions are involved in conspecific recognition or might increase predation risk. This study explores this dual role in the natterjack toad, Epidalea calamita (Laurenti, 1768), assessing whether secretions are involved in sex recognition and whether their emission carries a predation cost. To do this, we conducted 2 complementary experiments: The first assessed the behavioral responses of males and females to conspecific secretions and a control, and the second measured predator attacks on plasticine models impregnated with male or female secretions. Results showed that females spent significantly more time in areas with male secretions, suggesting attraction to these cues, while males showed no clear preference. At the same time, plasticine models treated with male secretions received significantly more predator attacks than those with female secretions. These findings suggest that male chemical signals in E. calamita may function as attractive sexual cues for females but also increase detectability by predators, pointing to a potential evolutionary trade-off between sexual attraction and predation risk mediated by chemical communication in this species.
title: The price of perfume: chemical communication and predation risk in an anuran

abstract: International scholars of fragmented musical sources gathered in the resplendent St Patrick’s College, Maynooth University for a conference entitled ‘Fragmented musical cultures c.1150–c.1350’, which ran on 15 and 16 May 2026 as part of the European Research Council project BROKENSONG. The conference, generously funded by the European Research Council, was organized by Karen Desmond, Eric Nemarich, Johanna-Pauline Thöne and Inês Trindade. Outside of the sessions, delegates were treated to a visit to the chapel, where John O’Keefe revealed more about the history of the seminary, followed by a showcase of the capabilities and colours of the immense chapel organ. Delegates also collaborated and exchanged ideas over a dinner at Barberstown Castle, Straffan. The venue for the conference and its surroundings were welcoming, and the delegates were greatly appreciative of the hospitality and refreshments provided by the hosts. BROKENSONG is a 5-year research project based at Maynooth University and funded by an European Research Council Consolidator Grant, for which Karen Desmond is the principal investigator. The project’s official title, ‘Polyphonic singing and communities of music writing in medieval Britain and Ireland, c.1150–1350’, encompasses the main angles taken by papers in the conference, spanning palaeographical and codicological analysis, as well as musicological investigation. The project is at its halfway point, running from 2023 to 2028. The sessions had an overarching focus on materiality, which allowed papers that explored a wide variety of sources, all of which are to some extent fragmentary. Sources ranged from new discoveries that will add to the polyphonic repertoire to chant fragments used to unpack new evidence of liturgical rites as well as illustrating arguments about reuse. Other sources included trouvère song and diverse liturgical materials. The focus of the conference on materiality was designed to suggest new lenses through which technologies of music making can be assessed. In the context of medieval song, these technologies could be the making of music books, the use of particular sources in performance or the repurposing of fragmentary sources for other aims, such as in a bookbinding. The conference theme also facilitated discussion about the fragmentary evidence of networks of musical exchange, music literacy in the Middle Ages and the layers of interaction found on a fragment source, especially one containing music. Papers that were focused on chant and monophonic sources engaged with ideas of materiality in a variety of ways, often linked with the context the use (or reuse) of a source. Jemima Bennett unpacked the fragments containing chant that were found in late-medieval Oxford bindings to continue the conversation about the reuse of musical fragments, while Emily Korzeniewski uncovered early examples of pedagogical vocal exercises in a source from San Zeno of Pistoia. The performance evidence from liturgical sources was elucidated by Alison Anstatt’s discussion of the ritual of foot washing as performed by nuns as well as by Eleonora Celora’s tracing of the cult of St Clement through a rhymed office in St Maur des Fossés in France. Materiality in chant sources also centred on themes of notational practice and the way in which this interacts with other aspects of the source. Jennifer Bain (in collaboration with Margot Fassler) introduced a quantitative methodology developed through the large-scale study of South German sources, which will soon enable researchers to date and locate chant sources more closely with the use of a forthcoming database that tracks individual features and differences between neumes across a single source. These tools will allow the palaeographical approach to chant sources with neumes to parallel that of analysing letter forms. Bain’s paper highlighted the importance of fragmentary sources in providing a vast number of samples across institutions to facilitate more in-depth comparison. The sequence repertoire and its notational intricacies were discussed by Jack Stebbing in an analytical deep dive into Laetabundus exsultet fidelis chorus; his presentation, illustrated by performance, showed the way in which the writing of a source is intrinsically linked to the orality and theoretical framework of the musicians interacting with it and how, as a result of this, melodic differences can occur. Turning to sources from France, Áine Palmer highlighted the role of notation in Bien mont amors entrepris, in which a tenor had been added to a monophonic songbook in order to fill space in the manuscript, thus hybridizing the form of both the song and the manuscript itself. Matthew Thomson explored the way in which scribal copying can be examined in the context of its surroundings and how scribes are guided by comparisons between exemplars, their memory and their knowledge of the repertoire when recording the melodic contours of songs. Other prevalent themes that emerged throughout the conference were discovery and reconstruction, especially in polyphonic sources. Mark Everist unveiled a discovery to the conference: a new fragmentary source, now in Berlin. This source raises questions about how books travelled and about cultural exchange in the time of the Black Prince, as well as exploring the implications of English books in a French-ruled Gascony. This session, and others, identified suitable methods for working with sources that had suffered damage or loss and highlighted opportunities for reconstruction. Lisa Colton re-examined evidence about female musicianship and music making in the convents of Sopwell and Wherwell. Exploring further north, Philippa Ovenden reassessed the sources that could link two compositions to Orkney, with historiographical discussions concerning the cult of St Magnus and a possible Orcadian Minorite monastery. Peter Lefferts revealed new discoveries at Lambeth Palace Library, where strips of polyphonic manuscripts had been found reused as sewing guards in a 1480s incunabulum. Jared Hartt presented on a collection of fragments within Oxford, New College MS 362, reconstructing the original gathering structure of what must originally have been a source containing a large number of polyphonic items. The wide range of papers presented at this two-day conference in Maynooth was a welcome reminder that collaboration and curiosity provide the impetus for innovation in the field of medieval and renaissance musicological research on early musical cultures and their sources. The programme facilitated in-depth scrutiny on certain reconstructions of sources, as well as inviting scholars to approach fragmentary manuscripts by using methods they may not have previously considered. The conference brought together established scholars and early-career researchers to further foster a communicative and driven research community that will continue to expand and flourish.
title: Music fragments conference in Maynooth

abstract: Communication signals of many taxa, such as coloration, differ in urban areas compared to natural habitats. However, the mechanisms shaping these divergences-genetic or environmental-remain unclear. We studied urban and forest great tits (Parus major) from populations where carotenoid-based coloration is reduced in urban habitats compared to forest, and first examined whether they differed in their melanic patches. We then used a common garden experiment to determine if the color differences were maintained when birds were raised from the unincubated egg stage in a common environment. In the wild, urban males showed smaller black ties than forest males, and along an urbanization gradient within urban habitat. Common garden birds of urban origin exhibited reduced chromatic yellow breast and smaller ties compared to forest-origin birds. In contrast, common garden birds from both habitats did not differ in yellow brightness or ultraviolet chroma. These results suggest that divergences in carotenoid saturation and melanin patch are primarily driven by genetic changes or early maternal investment in eggs, whereas yellow brightness or ultraviolet chroma are more environmentally determined. These findings provide information on the mechanisms driving phenotypic divergence in urban birds, with potential implications for mate choice, social dynamics, and evolutionary trajectories in anthropogenic landscapes.
title: Unmasking black and yellow in a common garden: genetic and environmental drivers of urban color divergence

abstract: Urbanization drastically changes our planet, and persistence in urban areas requires species to adapt. Sexual signaling has been argued to be a driver of population divergence between urban and non-urban populations, but it is often unclear whether population divergence is adaptive and caused by plastic and/or genetic processes. Calling behavior of urban and forest túngara frogs (Engystomops pustulosus) provides a well-known example of urban adaptation. However, we lack insight into the underlying genetic divergence between populations and heritability of calling behavior. Our aim was to examine the relative contributions of plastic and genetic components to urban-forest differences in sexual signaling and associated morphological traits. We reared frogs of urban and forest descent in a common garden using a paternal half-sib breeding design and used quantitative genetic approaches informed by whole-genome sequencing to estimate heritability. We show heritable urban-forest differences in call rate and amplitude (depending on the social environment), and in body size and condition. Moreover, behavioral as well as morphological traits had low to moderate heritability estimates. Our study provides insights into the underlying mechanisms of urban versus forest phenotypic divergence and suggests that sexual signaling and associated morphological traits in túngara frogs have the potential to adaptively evolve.
title: Heritable differences in sexual signaling and morphology between urban and forest túngara frogs

abstract: Abstract An expectation of a hypothesis that proposes cell-to-cell signaling pathways are redundant due to the redundancy of pathway terminal transcription factors (TFs) was tested by screening 35 signaling ligands for rescue of a decapentaplegic (dpp) hypomorphic wing growth phenotype. Three examples of partial rescue were identified: Hedgehog (HH), Semaphorin 1a (SEMA1A), and Wnt ortholog 2 (WNT2). HH overexpression with dppGAL4 may increase the expression of DPP from the hypomorphic dpp alleles. However, SEMA1A and WNT2 did not phenocopy the ectopic expression of HH or DPP, and neither SEMA1A nor WNT2 were required for wing growth, suggesting substitution of DPP for restoration of wing growth. The WNT2 rescue was dependent on the Frizzled 4 WNT receptor excluding the possibility that WNT2 weakly binds the DPP receptor. Although examples of phenotypic nonspecificity of signaling ligand function were identified, this is an expectation, and not direct proof, of the hypothesis of TF redundancy.
title: Rescue of a decapentaplegic hypomorphic wing growth phenotype by expression of the signaling ligands Hedgehog, Semaphorin a1, and Wnt homolog 2 in Drosophila melanogaster

abstract: Biological invasions are rarely examined through a locomotor lens, yet they provide a powerful opportunity to understand how organisms adjust movement in response to novel environmental conditions. When locomotion is considered in invasion biology, it is typically evaluated in terms of performance (e.g., speed, endurance, dispersal capacity), with far less attention given to how organisms restructure the behaviors that comprise locomotion itself. Urban environments introduce novel substrate geometries and mechanical challenges, potentially altering not only how animals move, but which behaviors they use. Using previously collected positional behavior data from an introduced population of monk parakeets (Myiopsitta monachus), this study evaluates how locomotor repertoire structure varies across substrate types, with particular emphasis on artificial substrates. Locomotor behavior was quantified as substrate-specific probability distributions and analyzed using complementary metrics of diversity, evenness, behavioral enrichment, and repertoire dissimilarity. Artificial substrates exhibited the highest locomotor diversity and high evenness, indicating a broad and relatively balanced use of locomotor behaviors. In contrast, natural substrates were characterized by lower diversity and greater dominance of specific behaviors. Behavioral enrichment analyses revealed increased use of walking and multiple climbing strategies on artificial substrates, coupled with reductions in aerial transitions (i.e, Flight_short_interbranch) and sidling. Dissimilarity metrics further demonstrated that locomotor repertoires on artificial substrates were qualitatively distinct from those observed in natural contexts. These findings indicate that urban environments drive restructuring of locomotor repertoires rather than simple performance tuning within a fixed behavioral framework. By demonstrating that locomotor behavior itself can shift in response to environmental novelty, this study highlights the importance of integrating behavioral, performance, and morphological perspectives when evaluating adaptation to urban environments and biological invasion.
title: Urban Invasion Restructures Locomotor Repertoires: Evidence from Introduced Monk Parakeets ( Myiopsitta monachus )

abstract: Abstract For some floating offshore wind designs, turbines can be disconnected and towed to port for major component replacement, but the ecological effects of these operations remain unknown. This study investigates the relationship between underwater noise levels and harbour porpoise occurrence and potential foraging activity during the tow-to-port maintenance of turbines at Hywind Scotland. Passive acoustic click detectors were deployed along a gradient array from the wind farm, with broadband recorders positioned at two locations along the array. Sound pressure levels (derived from one-third octave bands spanning 25 Hz to 40 kHz) increased significantly during large-scale maintenance, particularly during towing and mooring work, with peaks up to 29 dB above routine operational averages. Concurrently, porpoise detections declined, particularly within 2 km of a turbine, with reductions of up to 33% at 600 m from the nearest turbine during periods of large-scale maintenance compared to routine operations. Detection rates increased once high-intensity activities ceased, suggesting effects were temporary. Potential foraging activity showed no consistent change, indicating that porpoises likely continued to forage when present. These findings provide the first evidence of ecological responses to tow-to-port maintenance at a floating wind farm and suggest that disturbance may be short-lived and spatially restricted. However, this may change as wind farm size increases, as maintenance operations are likely to involve more turbines and vessels, potentially extending the duration and spatial extent of disturbance. As floating offshore wind developments expand in size, continued monitoring will be essential to assess cumulative and longer-term impacts of maintenance activities and to support effective environmental management.
title: Impacts of large-scale maintenance of a floating offshore wind farm on noise levels and harbour porpoise activity

abstract: Abstract In the southwest Indian Ocean (SWIO), the Mascarene region has been identified as an Important Marine Mammals Area, yet the seasonal use of these waters by large baleen whales remains poorly resolved. We analysed passive acoustic data from 16 Ocean Bottom Seismometers deployed from October 2012 to November 2013 across latitudinal and longitudinal transects around Réunion Island and off eastern Madagascar. Songs of fin whales (Balaenoptera physalus), Antarctic blue whales (B. m. intermedia), and SWIO/Madagascar pygmy blue whales (B. m. brevicauda) were manually annotated from spectrograms to quantify hourly acoustic presence per day. Fin whales showed the highest acoustic presence among the three studied taxa, with seasonal presence lasting up to 8 months (April–December) and clear north–south patterns in the onset and end of acoustic presence. Antarctic blue whales were detected less frequently, primarily during austral autumn and winter, with records extending north to 16°S and secondary peaks in October–November consistent with southward movement after wintering farther north. Madagascar pygmy blue whales showed a pronounced bimodal acoustic presence (mid-October–mid-January; March–July/August) and a strong longitudinal structuring, with greater acoustic presence in the western part of the study area. The spatial distribution differed markedly between these two periods, revealing distinct migration pathways through the region during northward and southward movements. Taken together, these results identify the Mascarene waters as a shared seasonal habitat for fin whales, Antarctic blue whales, and Madagascar pygmy blue whales, while highlighting distinct seasonal and spatial patterns among taxa. Given the intense shipping activity in the region, continued and expanded acoustic monitoring is needed to assess long-term whale habitat use, characterize underwater noise, and evaluate its potential influence on the use of these waters, thereby informing future conservation measures.
title: Seasonal acoustic presence of blue and fin whales in the Mascarene waters (southwestern Indian Ocean)

abstract: On 17 September 2024, the ICSID Tribunal in Odyssey Marine Exploration, Inc v United Mexican States (Award) (hereafter Odyssey) issued its decision related to deep seabed mining, with a particular focus on dredging permits. This case comment identifies three critical observations arising from the Award that shed light on broader debates in investment arbitration. First, the decision highlights the challenges associated with third-party interventions in investor–State dispute settlement (ISDS) proceedings, particularly in environmental matters that involve a ‘public interest’ element affecting both local communities and the environment. Second, it exposes the Tribunal’s failure to adequately situate the dispute within a broader international legal framework, including relevant principles of environmental law, ISDS jurisprudence and the law governing deep seabed mining. In this respect, the Award illustrates how future deep seabed mining disputes may generate tensions between investors and environmental protection. Third, the Award raises serious concerns regarding the risk of double recovery, demonstrating how the international investment regime may unduly empower investors3 to bring claims against States even where justice has already been served by domestic courts, or while domestic judicial proceedings remain pending. Against this background, the case comment is structured as follows: Section II provides the factual background of the dispute. Section III outlines the findings of the Majority (composed of Mr Felipe Bulnes Serrano and Dr Stanimir Alexandrov). Section IV offers reflections on the Award, including an analysis of the dissenting opinion of Professor Philippe Sands, KC. By way of analogy with the Greek mythological tale, the comment examines how the Tribunal navigated through these three critical legal issues in what may be described as a ‘lost Odyssey’. Section V concludes. The dispute began when Odyssey Marine Exploration, Inc, a firm incorporated in Nevada, United States, brought a claim against Mexico under the North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA),4 with the administrative centre being ICSID, for its subsidiary incorporated in Mexico. Odyssey had been preparing for deep seabed mining activities off the coast of the Baja California Peninsula, in the Gulf of Ulloa, where it obtained a mining concession in 2012 for an area exceeding 2680 km2.5 The goal of the mining project was the exploitation of sedimentary phosphate deposits, which are vital minerals for the energy transition.6 In order for Odyssey’s Mexican subsidiary to begin deep seabed mining operations, it was required to submit an environmental impact assessment (EIA) to the relevant public authority, SEMARNAT, which is responsible for overseeing natural resources.7 Odyssey submitted two separate EIAs during the process. The first EIA was submitted but returned by SEMARNAT for further clarification regarding mitigation measures related to species and biodiversity protection, and clarification regarding technical inconsistencies.8 SEMARNAT ultimately denied permission for dredging activities, citing both environmental and technical concerns associated with deep seabed mining. The rejection decision also highlighted significant risks to five migratory species, including the endangered Caretta caretta (loggerhead sea turtle), whose survival is threatened due to their limited geographical distribution.9 Odyssey appealed this first denial to the Federal Administrative Tribunal (FAT).10 The FAT annulled SEMARNAT’s decision and criticised the agency for failing to provide adequate reasons for denying the dredging permit, particularly in relation to the five listed species.11 Subsequently, the FAT requested a reassessment of the proposal in light of additional information submitted by Odyssey as part of a second application for dredging permission. However, SEMARNAT once again rejected the request.12 This second rejection was also appealed in 2019, but by the time the Tribunal was constituted and even by the time the Award was released in September 2024, the appeal had not yet been handed down.13 Despite the ongoing appeal, Odyssey filed a claim under NAFTA, alleging a breach of the fair and equitable treatment (FET) standard due to the failure to grant the necessary dredging permission. Odyssey alleged that the rejection of permits was politically motivated and manipulated by the Secretary of SEMARNAT, Mr Pachianno, for personal and political reasons. After confirming that the FET standard under Article 1105(1) of NAFTA should be interpreted in accordance with the Interpretative Notes of the NAFTA Free Trade Commission, which are binding on any tribunal constituted under NAFTA, the Tribunal determined that the FET standard aligned with customary international law.14 Accordingly, a breach of the FET occurs if the conduct of the public authority is ‘arbitrary, grossly unfair, unjust or idiosyncratic, discriminatory, exposes the claimant to sectional or racial prejudice, or involves a lack of due process leading to an outcome which offends judicial propriety’, as stated in Waste Management v Mexico (II).15 The Majority found that the initial denial of the permit was due to personal interference by the Secretary of SEMARNAT, Mr Pachianno, who allegedly instructed SEMARNAT employees to reject the permit based on the testimony of two former employees, Mr Flores and Mr Villa, who were paid by Odyssey as witnesses—a practice not unusual in investment arbitration.16 According to the Majority, the rejection was not driven by genuine environmental concerns but by personal motives, which rendered the decision arbitrary and unfair. One of the central points of dissent by Professor Philippe Sands, KC, was his view that Mexico’s refusal to grant the permit was grounded in a broader, more holistic approach to environmental protection, rather than in narrow or purely procedural considerations (see Section IV).17 This conclusion was supported by the FAT’s first ruling, which criticised the initial rejection for lacking environmental and scientific support.18 Mr Pachianno denied the allegations.19 However, the Majority also relied on the fact that SEMARNAT publicly stated, shortly after the first rejection, that it would deny Odyssey’s renewed application for dredging activities within five days of the FAT’s ruling, thus acting arbitrarily.20 Taking all these factors into account, the Majority concluded that the denial of permits, allegedly influenced by Mr Pachianno, was attributable to Mexico, and thus constituted a breach of the FET standard under Article 1105(1) of NAFTA, even though the appeal process regarding the second rejection was still ongoing at the time.21 It is noteworthy that the Majority found a breach of the FET standard under Article 1105(1) of NAFTA, despite the fact that the Mexican judiciary had full control over the review process for the denial of permissions, as clearly demonstrated by the annulment of the first rejection decision. This approach was criticised in the dissenting opinion of Professor Philippe Sands, KC, who disagreed with the Majority’s finding that the FET standard had been breached, arguing that the actions were neither ‘shocking’ nor ‘arbitrary’.22 The Award and the dissent provide three key points of reflection, offering a critical analysis of the Majority’s decision.23 Third-party interventions may play an important role in ISDS, as they can indirectly promote environmental protection and sustainable development objectives.24 In the present case, there were two third-party interventions: one by the Center for International Environmental Law (CIEL) and another by the Sociedad Cooperativa de Producción Pesquera Puerto Chale (Cooperativa). These entities sought to present factual and legal arguments concerning the potential impacts of deep seabed mining on surrounding communities (particularly fishing communities) as well as on the marine environment in the Gulf of Ulloa.25 The Majority of the Tribunal denied permission for these third parties to intervene, stating that they had nothing to contribute to the arbitration proceedings.26 In doing so, the Majority failed to give adequate consideration to the potential role of third-party submissions,27 in providing relevant factual, legal and technical information regarding the environmental effects of deep seabed mining off the coast of the Baja California Peninsula.28 Professor Philippe Sands, KC, strongly dissented from the Majority’s decision to refuse these interventions.29 He stated that the: unique perspective [of CIEL and Cooperativa] would have been extremely valuable, and [it is] deeply regrettable that the Majority has decided that it does not wish to hear from a community that is directly affected by the outcome of the proceedings. Such a decision will only serve to undermine perceptions as the legitimacy of these proceedings.30 These interventions would have provided expert opinions explaining why Mexico refused to grant the permit for deep seabed mining, reinforcing the idea that Western or Global North companies are significant drivers of such mining activities.31 The Majority isolated the dispute at hand from environmental law more broadly by adopting a narrow view, holding that the environmental NGOs failed to demonstrate a significant interest in the dispute or that they could provide meaningful assistance to the Tribunal.32 Amici curiae have traditionally been used in matters involving public policy and public interest, such as environmental protection, public health or cultural heritage.33 Allowing amici to participate may enhance the legitimacy of arbitral proceedings.34 This is because it counterbalances the inherent logic of ISDS, which entails the confidential review of State conduct (conduct that often concerns matters of public interest), thereby limiting broader systemic accountability.35 This approach to confidentiality has also been criticised by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development.36 At the same time, the admission of prospective amici should not prejudice the outcome of the proceedings. From another perspective, as Ridi argues, amicus interventions are unlikely to succeed if the prospective amici cannot offer insights beyond those that experienced counsel could provide, a point echoed by the Majority in Odyssey.37 Ridi further observed that Odyssey illustrates a situation where the prospective amici appeared primarily to support Mexico’s position, rather than to assist the Tribunal in its deliberations.38 Even though this point is valid, the issues must also be viewed within the broader systemic context for ISDS, a regime currently facing significant challenges. In this regard, amici could serve, at least in part, to restore public trust in the system. Factually and legally, they may illuminate and remind tribunals of the broader normative framework of international law within which awards are rendered, consistent with Article 38(1)(d) of the Statute of the International Court of Justice. Admittedly, opening proceedings to public interest perspectives may prolong the process, but it would likely strengthen the perceived legitimacy of the outcome. This is essentially a question of which policy considerations should prevail. This is not to suggest that the conditions for admission as amicus curiae should be disregarded. However, the NAFTA Statement on Non-Disputing Party Participation39 includes an additional ‘public interest’40 element, which is clearly present in this case. Although tribunals retain discretion to admit amicus curiae submissions (third parties have no inherent right of participation),41 a restrictive approach in cases involving significant public interests risks overlooking the broader normative context within which ISDS operates. By excluding third-party interventions, the Tribunal missed the opportunity to consider statements and perspectives from NGOs regarding the environmental implications of deep seabed mining. An overly strict approach may prevent the Tribunal from taking into account important considerations, particularly in cases involving environmental protection. Connected to the preceding issue, a broader systemic concern arises from the narrow positioning of the case. This narrowness may be viewed as increasing the trench between international investment law and its interaction with other international legal regimes. In recent years, deep seabed mining has attracted increasing attention, particularly as activities have begun shifting from the exploration phase towards the potential extraction of critical rare earth minerals, such as ferromanganese nodules. Conversely, from the perspective of the law of the sea, States parties to the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS) are under an obligation to prevent environmental harm and marine pollution, including harm arising from activities such as deep seabed mining.42 However, the Majority found that Mexico had not enacted environmental regulations per se, but rather that the rejection of permits was procedurally flawed. This raises important questions about the repercussions this case may have for future arbitration proceedings concerning deep seabed mining, specifically, whether the protection of investors will continue to prevail over the protection of the environment. These concerns are especially relevant in light of increasing calls within the deep seabed mining regime for a precautionary pause or moratorium until the Mining Code is finalised.43 Instead of prioritising investors’ rights as a starting point, the Tribunal should have placed the focus on the Gulf of Ulloa and its marine environment as the primary subject of legal protection. This view is reinforced by the fact that the Majority failed to engage with Mexico’s environmental obligations, and regrettably, Mexico itself did not advance such arguments. A nature-centred approach, guided by the precautionary principle, could have led to a different outcome.44 Similarly, by neglecting Mexico’s obligations under customary international law to preserve biodiversity and protect the environment, the Tribunal did not fully engage with the principle of systemic integration, as reflected in Article 31(3)(c) of the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties (VCLT).45 Although neither disputing party expressly referred to the VCLT or to the principle of systemic integration when assessing the alleged breach of the FET standard,46 this may have constituted a missed opportunity for Mexico to invoke its customary international law obligations to protect and preserve the environment. As a result, the Tribunal may have lacked a sufficient basis to engage with this broader systemic-oriented approach to legal reasoning. Such an approach, which adjudicators ought to adopt, would have required consideration of relevant developments in international environmental law, including the significance of resolutions adopted by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) at its World Conservation Congress. These resolutions called for a moratorium on deep seabed mining exploitation, addressing its 170 Member States and more than 1400 IUCN member organisations.47 The Mexican State supported this moratorium, and yet it is now required to pay compensation. This outcome illustrates the consequences of an anthropocentric approach to international investment law, one that prioritises property rights and the interests of investors while relegating environmental considerations to a secondary position.48 Moreover, Mexico is a member of the Deep Sea Conservation Coalition, together with more than 40 States, all of which support a moratorium on deep seabed extraction until adequate mining regulations are adopted by the International Seabed Authority.49 Several of these points were raised in the third-party interventions discussed in the preceding section. This underscores the role of such interventions in illuminating the broader international legal context and reminding tribunals of their duty to operate within the wider framework of international law, particularly in light of contemporary challenges and evolving global realities. Notably, the Majority did not even refer to the VCLT, which is a missed opportunity. As such, it is a missed opportunity for the Tribunal to integrate a non-anthropocentric view into ISDS. A more integrated approach, one that acknowledged the environmental risks and potential harm posed by deep seabed mining, would have provided a more balanced and legally sound outcome, especially in light of the strong emphasis on protecting the environment in this day and age. In investment arbitration, there is a potential risk of double recovery, particularly where multiple or ongoing proceedings are taking place in the host State that may result in the State compensating the foreign investor more than once.50 This is a pressing issue and is typically raised by the respondent State. It is also relevant in the present case, as Mexico invoked this concern in light of the ongoing domestic court proceedings. As Professor Philippe Sands, KC, succinctly observed in his dissent,51 the Mexican legal system was functioning properly. One judicial body annulled the first rejection, and the second rejection remains under appeal in the Mexican courts. In the first case, justice was served. However, what happens if the second judicial decision also annuls the second rejection, even though Odyssey has already secured an international Award of US$37.1 million?52 This scenario raises significant concerns regarding double recovery, contrary to the general principle of international law enunciated in the Factory of Chorzów case, which underscored avoiding risks ‘of the same damage being compensated twice’.53 In this case, the mere risk of double compensation arising from both the Tribunal’s Award and potential domestic court proceedings is sufficient to warrant attention. Nevertheless, the issue of double recovery was addressed by the Majority.54 The Majority, however, appeared to accept uncritically the claimant investor’s submissions in their post-hearing brief,55 which relied heavily on the reasoning in Chevron v Ecuador.56 That case similarly argued that the risk of double recovery should not be because domestic a outcome for the claimant The claimant investor argued that the second rejection, which was under appeal, would to and the of a deep seabed mining permit the that the arguments of double recovery were and to a on Chevron v the that concerns regarding double recovery are not matters for international tribunals to on the or phase but should be addressed in the of a case, or after the Award has been The further v which that risks of double recovery in of proceedings should be with by domestic courts. title: Odyssey Marine Exploration v United Mexican States: Three Critical Issues in Troubled Waters

abstract: In A Marginal Sea (2022), a collection of poetry written from the vantage point of Ynys Môn (Anglesey), an island in the marginal sea of the Atlantic off the northwest coast of Wales, Zoë Skoulding attends to the sonic senses to address anthropogenic climate change.1 Sounding the porous borders between languages and cultures, Skoulding’s mode of expansive listening tunes in to a range of animal, vegetal, and mineral frequencies. In this essay, by tracing the passages between the local and the global, and the personal and the planetary, I suggest that Skoulding sounds the relationship between language and ecology and in so doing develops an archipelagic “poethics” that allows both connection and difference to resonate. Drawing on Joan Retallack’s notion of a “poethics” that resists “delimiting forms” and offers instead a “swerve” (38) toward the “unknown,” “otherness,” and “unintelligibility” (22), this essay is interested in what takes place at the limits of the audible in Skoulding’s writing, and how, by tuning in to alternative frequencies, the work engages with archipelagic perspectives and more-than-human ecologies. Recognizing the political as well as the aesthetic dimensions of auditory culture, my approach extends Skoulding’s own analysis of noise in Poetry and Listening, in which she argues, citing Retallack: “The verge of noticing is the verge of knowledge; this is the point at which listening operates” (Skoulding 10). Pointing out that silence signals not an absence of sound but rather the limits of cultural intelligibility, Skoulding extends the work of Retallack outwards, situating the poem within the social, technological, and more-than-human world that it both reflects and shapes. Challenging the interpretation of lyric expression as “a singular transmission from mouth to ear, or from inner speech to inner ear,” Skoulding argues that “the dispersal of lyric into noisier, more interrupted forms enables the expression of new subjectivities that encompass the non-human and post-human” (13). Discussing the human and nonhuman soundscapes of A Marginal Sea in this essay, I ask what her sonic exploration of Ynys Môn and its geographically and textually connected sites—their excessive noises as well as their unintelligible silences—can tell us about the role of listening in opening up ways of relating to the earth that move beyond fixed cultural, national, and linguistic borders and nurturing a more “poethical” relation to the planet. In so doing, I explore how Skoulding develops modes of auditory engagement that invite the reader—in the words of Retallack—to adopt “a certain poetics of responsibility with the courage of the swerve” (3). This essay consists of two parts. First, I consider the experimental interplay between languages and environments in A Marginal Sea. Extending existing scholarship on her writing on place, I ask how the notion of “islandness” informs Skoulding’s practice, noting that A Marginal Sea is always entangled and shaped through its connection to other places. Drawing on Peter Barry, I consider modes of “peripheral listening” across and between Skoulding’s poems, where translingual and more-than-human frequencies expand modes of attunement to island ecologies. Second, I turn to the work of Édouard Glissant to deepen my analysis of Skoulding’s archipelagic soundings, suggesting that thinking with Glissant opens up ways of reading moments in Skoulding’s work where the boundaries between land and sea, between stone and sky, and between language and rock, are productively—and sometimes noisily—blurred. Operating within a different kind of marginality, one that is neither equivalent to nor entirely separate from the postcolonial dynamics that Glissant theorizes, I suggest that by reading Skoulding alongside Glissant, one might develop a more nuanced understanding of how expanded listening reconfigures place, thereby reframing the earth as both ground and opening. In “If Anyone Asks,” Skoulding’s prose poem from A Marginal Sea, words themselves are “like an island on the edge of an island” (32), where an Odyssean wayfarer finds himself “sailing the wine-blue to peoples of alien speech,” navigating “weather systems” while surrounded by “translucent fish and islands in luminous water” (32). The soliloquy was originally composed as part of a collaborative work with the Welsh poet Nia Davies entitled “Mare Nostrum” (“Our Sea”), the Latin name used by the Roman empire to describe the Mediterranean at the height of its imperial power. In reclaiming the phrase, Davies and Skoulding bring it into dialogue with the Italian naval rescue mission of the same name, launched in October 2013 following the Lampedusa shipwreck in which 366 people—primarily from Eritrea, Somalia, and Ethiopia—lost their lives. Crucially, Operation Mare Nostrum was the first such mission whose specific mandate was to rescue people at sea rather than solely to reinforce Europe’s border regime (Cuttitta 638). By naming their collaboration after this operation, the two poets invoke questions about territory, nomenclature, and the rights to cross a sea that others have claimed as their own. “If Anyone Asks,” Skoulding’s contribution to the collaboration as it appears in A Marginal Sea, speaks to what Giorgio Agamben would call the bare life of those seeking asylum (4)—those reduced, in the poem’s own phrase, to an “assemblage of cells” (Skoulding 32). The poem opens with an imperative that is at once survival strategy and political provocation: “Say you are nobody” (32), Skoulding writes, calling up the nameless numbers of populist anti-immigration rhetoric, in which the specificity of individual lives is replaced by the counted but unheard. At the same time, she reaches back to Homer’s epic, invoking the episode in Book IX when Odysseus tells the Cyclops “My name is Nobody” (9.365–6), a ploy that allows him to escape by making the report of his violence unnameable. When Polyphemus cries out that “Nobody” has hurt him (9.408), the neighboring Cyclopes retreat. The language of the denial thus becomes the mechanism of survival. Skoulding’s retelling, however, inverts this Homeric logic. Where Odysseus chooses anonymity as a tactic, asserting his real name once safely out of reach, the refugees in the poem are assigned anonymity by a system that refuses to name them. And where Odysseus is aided throughout his wanderings by a divine protector, here the “grey-eyed Athene went away with the likeness of a vulture” (Skoulding 32) and her heroes are denied passage rather than receiving guidance from the gods. Transitioning from the past to the present tense in “it was nobody my name is nobody” (32), Skoulding collapses the distinction between the ancient epic and the contemporary politics of exclusion. This collapse of temporal and textual registers is central to how the poem operates. Combining Homeric epic, the official language of a British passport, and the grammar of contemporary media, the poem holds multiple intertexts in uncomfortable tension. The statement reprinted in all British passports and reproduced in Skoulding’s poem—“to allow the bearer to pass freely without let or hindrance” (32)—sits alongside the image of people “struggling up the sides of the ship with ropes and ladders their hands and feet were cut and slipping” (33). abstract: Conspicuous sexual signals are frequently under selection from conflicting sources, such as natural versus sexual selection and precopulatory versus postcopulatory sexual selection, which may act in the same or different directions. The Pacific field cricket (Teleogryllus oceanicus) is undergoing rapid evolutionary trait loss: mutations that render males obligately silent (the "flatwing phenotype") have become established on several islands of Hawai'i. Females strongly discriminate against silent males, yet flatwings do gain matings. In this study, we take advantage of this natural system to understand how investment in ejaculate quality under high and low perceived sperm competition risk (manipulated using acoustic cues) differs between wild type males and flatwings, which obligately adopt alternative reproductive tactics (ARTs). We replicated our study in two islands with different flatwing frequencies because female mating rate and therefore sperm competition risk is likely higher in O'ahu than Kaua'i. We measured testes mass and gene expression for three seminal fluid proteins (SFPs) that affect paternity success, sperm viability, and female propensity to remate. Compared to Kaua'i males, O'ahu males showed higher residual testes mass and expression of ToSfp011, which increases male sperm viability and paternity success, and reduces mate searching behaviour by females. We found no effect of immediate sperm competition risk or wing morph on any of the SFPs or testes mass. Differential SFP expression and residual testes mass in Hawaiian populations that likely differ in mating rate are compatible with the predictions of sperm competition theory.
title: Ejaculate investment differs by population, but not wing morph or perceived sperm competition risk, in Pacific field crickets.

abstract: The ecological impact of Bombus terrestris (Linnaeus, 1758) (Hymenoptera: Apidae) following its introduction to regions outside its native range has raised significant concerns, particularly regarding the decline of native pollinators. Male B. terrestris secrete pheromones that are used in reproductive communication, and which have the potential to be used as trap attractants to control invasive populations. However, while gynes (virgin reproductive females) are known to be attracted to these pheromones, nothing is known about behavioral responses of male B. terrestris to them. Here, we investigated whether male B. terrestris exhibit attraction to pheromone extracts from conspecific males under controlled laboratory conditions. A Y-tube olfactometer was used to present B. terrestris males with a choice between a pheromone extract and a control treatment. Males were shown to respond to a positive control of lavender oil; however, they exhibited no attraction to the pheromone extracts. Several factors, such as pheromone concentration, age of individuals, or apparatus design, may have influenced these results. These findings contribute to our knowledge of bumblebee chemical communication and may inform future experimental design to assess pheromone attraction in bumblebees.
title: No evidence for male attraction to cephalic labial gland pheromones in Bombus terrestris (Hymenoptera: Apidae)

abstract: Cicadas are a group of insects recognized for their distinctive life cycle and the stridulatory calls produced by males to attract females. While cicadas are commonly associated with thermophilic forests and xerophilic shrublands in Mediterranean regions, their distribution in temperate areas of Europe remains poorly understood. This study focuses on the cicadas of the northern Iberian Peninsula, specifically Asturias, characterized by a temperate climate. Over three years of fieldwork, we surveyed potential sites to locate cicada populations. Efforts were made to collect data on their habitat, ecology, and behavior. Acoustic recordings were used to characterize species-specific calling songs, and specimens were captured for genetic analyses. In addition, species distribution models were developed using climatic variables to assess potential habitat suitability across the region. We identified four cicada taxa-Cicada orni, Tibicina quadrisignata, Tettigettalna argentata, and Cicadetta sp.-primarily occupying forested habitats, native shrublands, and pine plantations. These species were found between 200 and 1,600 m a.s.l. and were acoustically active at temperatures above 18 to 21 °C, preferentially during sunny and low-wind conditions. Distribution models highlighted the warmest valleys of the study area as the most favorable for cicada occurrence, providing guidance for future sampling efforts. Furthermore, we provide the first genetic characterization of the cicada species detected in the region, which supports the morphological and acoustic identifications and reveals the presence of a putative new species of the genus Cicadetta. Finally, we outline conservation-relevant considerations for the preservation of cicada populations in temperate environments.
title: Echoes from northern Iberia: distribution, ecology, genetics, and identification of Asturian cicadas (Hemiptera: Cicadidae)

abstract: Abstract Potential exaggeration in animal communication, though rare, challenges assumptions about the reliability of communication systems. While signals typically convey accurate information, some individuals may exaggerate their traits to gain competitive or reproductive advantages. Among mammals, scent and visual marks are primary communication modes, generally constrained by anatomy and expected to reflect body size honestly. However, manipulating these signals could help subadult or subordinate individuals avoid larger rivals. Using Cantabrian brown bears (Ursus arctos) as a model, we investigated exaggerated marking and its frequency. Over 117,552 h of camera-trap monitoring (2021 to 2024) at 14 marking sites, we recorded 164 individual bears. Seven males (4.3%) engaged in potentially exaggerated marking by climbing marking sites or using platforms to mark higher than their natural height. Of these, 57.1% were adults, and 42.9% were subadults. Elevated marking occurred at 14.3% of sites, mostly during the day. These findings suggest that brown bears can manipulate 'index signals' once considered unfakeable, adding complexity to their communication system. This study provides a cautious perspective on the dynamics of exaggerated signaling, offering insights into the evolutionary maintenance of honest communication systems in nature.
title: Exaggerated signaling in a solitary mammal: evidence from brown bears ( Ursus arctos )

abstract: Abstract Prey naivety is a major consideration in the recovery of endangered populations, particularly when reintroduction sites house predators with which prey have no prior exposure. Since the eradication of rinderpest in the early 2000s, population growth of the Critically Endangered Hirola (Beatragus hunteri) has been suppressed due to a combination of predation and habitat loss stemming from the conversion of grassland to shrubland. We expected that Hirola within a predator-free sanctuary would relax their anti-predator responses over time, particularly with respect to proactive behaviors like vigilance when compared to individuals from the surrounding Ishaqbini Community Conservancy (where predators are present). In 2 sampling periods (2013 to 2015, and 2020 to 2021), we conducted focal observations to quantify a proactive anti-predator response (time spent vigilant) and 3 reactive anti-predator responses (flight distance, time spent fleeing, flight speed) for Hirola groups within the 2 settings. Contrary to our central hypothesis, vigilance did not decline over time for Hirola from the predator-proof sanctuary. Instead, vigilance was maintained at approximately constant levels from 2013 to 2015 to 2020 to 2021, both for individuals in the sanctuary and individuals in the conservancy. Although flight distance did not differ between experimental settings, Hirola in the conservancy fled a simulated predator, Lion (Panthera leo), via roar playbacks ca. 5 times as quickly as Hirola within the sanctuary. Whether Hirola reintroduced from the predator-proof sanctuary experience increased mortality therefore could depend on whether and how effectively vigilance reduces predation risk. We recommend (i) reintroducing individuals to areas with low predator densities and (ii) regular monitoring of behavior and survivorship following release to enhance the outcome of future reintroductions, and to better understand how proactive and reactive anti-predator behaviors differentially shape individual survival.
title: Proactive and reactive anti-predator responses of exclosure-bred versus wild Hirola ( Beatragus hunteri ): implications for reintroductions and population recovery

abstract: Abstract Objective This study aims to address the effects of a difference in sex ratio on courtship behavior, egg production, egg hatching rate, and larval survival in Zebrafish Danio rerio, providing a theoretical basis for optimizing sex ratios in laboratory breeding conditions through systematic evaluation of the complete reproductive process from behavior to offspring viability. Methods Zebrafish broodstock (AB strain blue zebra) consisting of 15 males and 12 females (age = 7–9 months) were prepared, and two groups of fish with different sex ratios—female-biased (one male and two females [1M:2F group]) and male-biased (four males and two females [4M:2F group])—were set and allocated to breeding isolation devices for subsequent experiments. Results We compared courtship behavior, fecundity, and subsequent embryonic development. Behavioral observations showed that males in the 1M:2F group preferred a single female. The other female actively approached the male to seek stimulation, often interfering with normal courtship. In contrast, males in the 4M:2F group exhibited more intense courtship behavior, including various male–female chasing patterns, ensuring that females received sufficient stimulation. Regarding fecundity, the average egg production in the 1M:2F group was measured as 191 eggs/female, while the 4M:2F group demonstrated a mean egg count of 279 per female.
